en: The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The summary verse says:
Śāriputra’s renunciation, the two followers of external paths,
the young boy who drove away the crows, and the arhat’s sick woman.
The summary verse says:
The ordination of Śāriputra, The permission to receive full ordination;
The subduing of Cūḍapanthaka, And the five kinds of non-Buddhists.

At that time, there was a king of Campā named Aṅga, and there was also a neighboring king of Magadha known as Mahāpadma. Their two realms were adjacent to one another; both were densely populated, prosperous, peaceful, and secure, with formidable armies. They had been attacking and counter-attacking each other for many years, alternating between victory and defeat.

Later, at another time, King Aṅga, seeing that his kingdom was prosperous and its population abundant, recalled his old grievances. He immediately repaired his armor and prepared his troops, mobilizing a grand military force; he set a date and exhorted his assembly, intending to come together to exterminate [the enemy].
At that time, the frontier guards perceived this first and dispatched a messenger to inform the king. Upon hearing the news, the king mobilized his army to resist; the two forces engaged in combat.
Padmaka suffered defeat and withdrew his troops into the city, closing the gates to hold a firm defense.
At that time, King Aṅga was intent on subjugating him and sent an envoy with this message:
"If you surrender, it will be well;
if not, you shall never be spared."
Even if they were to leap into the air, nets would fly up to capture them;
even if they were to enter the water, they would be drawn in by sunken nets;
and even if they were to climb mountains or flee into forests, there would be no path of escape.
Upon hearing this, King Padmaka was seized with great fear and immediately addressed his ministers, saying:
"Now the army of Aṅga is powerful and a stern envoy has arrived; as the national crisis is profound, by what means may we be liberated from it?"
The ministers replied to the king, speaking in verse:
“Where there is a king, there is a kingdom; without a king, the kingdom does not endure.
A ruined kingdom may yet be restored, but once life has perished, it can never be renewed.”
"The fate of the state and that of the individual are two things that conflict; one should protect one's life well.
A ruined state may be re-established, but once life is severed, it is difficult to expect its return.

At that time, the ministers urged the king to surrender. The king followed their counsel, bound his own neck with chains, and went to the place of King Aṅga. There they established an alliance, pledging to pay taxes forevermore.
When these matters were completed, he was immediately released and returned home.
At that time, while the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he observed that there were five conditions present in the world, and he was about to descend to be born.

At that time, the devas of the six heavens of desire performed their respective duties; within the womb of Queen Māyā, purified three times over in the house of King Śuddhodana in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, they caused her to receive a most auspicious dream, in which she saw the Bodhisattva descending into her womb in the form of a white elephant.

At that time, the great earth shook, and a brilliant radiance shone forth, outshining the color of gold and pervading the entire world. Surpassing the orbs of the sun and moon, it extended upward as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; all was bright and transparently clear, such that every darkness was entirely dispelled.

Even if the sun and moon, despite their majestic radiance, previously left something unreached and could not distinguish it from the long-standing darkness, once they encounter this divine light, all shall be seen clearly.
However, the manifestations displayed by the Sage are not known to the world.
At that time, there were four great kings:
first, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was King Mahāpadma;
In the second city, Śrāvastī, there was the Great King Māra;
in the third city, Uśanī, the Great King Śatadru;
and in the fourth city, Kauśāmbī, the Great King Ānandanimi.
On the day the Bodhisattva descended into birth, these four kings each gave birth to a crown prince within their own inner palaces.
King Mahāpadma, having encountered a light upon the birth of his son, took it to be an auspicious sign for his child and thought to himself:
"The majesty and virtue of my son are like those of the rising sun."
"My son’s majestic radiance is able to illuminate the world.
Because his light and shadow were so exceptionally sublime, serving as a sign of auspiciousness, he was consequently named Prince Chāyā-jita (Shadow-Conquering).
At that time, King Māra was likewise like that king; taking that radiance as an auspicious omen for his son, he spoke these words:

"Now that this son of mine has first been born, the portents are most excellent and the radiance fills all around; the realm is peaceful and tranquil. It is fitting that we manifest his virtue by establishing a name."
Consequently, he was named Prince Jayasena.
At that time, King Śatānīka likewise regarded this as an auspicious omen for his son and spoke thus:
"My son possesses virtue and has manifested a radiance; it is fitting that I establish a name for him to commemorate this auspicious sign."
Consequently, he was named Prince Prabhaṃkara.
At that time, King Ānandadinna likewise regarded this as an auspicious omen for his son and spoke thus:
"My son has been born like the rising sun; spreading light to dispel darkness, his radiance ascends ever higher, manifesting a most excellent and auspicious sign."
Consequently, he was named Prince Āditya.

At that time, each of the four kings established names for their sons based on auspicious signs, none of whom knew that these were all manifestations of the great majestic spiritual power of the Śākya Bodhisattva.
However, all these princes had long accumulated superior causes and possessed great power of aspiration; each leading his own retinue, they were born following the Sage.

Thus, Bimbisāra appeared in accordance with the timing, emerging as an extraordinary man among men. Consequently, on the day of his birth, five hundred high ministers each gave birth to a son, who was named according to his respective clan.
As for Prince Bimbisāra, he was nurtured by eight nurses. As the days passed and the months accumulated, he grew like a lotus emerging from the water.

Regarding what he studied—scriptures, arts and crafts, calendrical calculations, and all the royal duties of a consecrated Kṣatriya king—he understood them all without exception. Furthermore, he devoted himself to the fields of technical skill, including the methods of training elephants and horses, driving chariots, drawing bows and discharging arrows, casting nooses, wielding swords, and treating wounds; he mastered all such arts.
Moreover, he thoroughly mastered the four branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) without leaving anything unlearned.
Together with the five hundred sons of the great ministers, they all likewise attained complete mastery.

Later, on another occasion, while the prince was acting as regent for the kingdom, he happened to travel by elephant during a period of leisure and saw people being subjected to the collection of taxes and levies.
He then asked his attendants,
"For what reason are these people seeking something?
They replied:
"He is an envoy from the King of Aṅga, a neighboring kingdom, who has come from afar to collect taxes. The Prince asked,
"For what reason must our country pay tribute to another?"
He replied, "It has been so for a long time. At that moment,
the Prince immediately summoned the messenger and questioned him, saying:
"The king of that country is a Kṣatriya consecrated by coronation, and I too am a Kṣatriya consecrated by coronation; yet our governance differs, and the people of each realm are distinct."
"For what reason have you crossed our borders and overstepped your limits to come here and demand [payment]? You should return at once;
from now on, let this matter be forever ended. Having heard this, the envoy thought to himself:
"This crown prince is by nature fierce and unruly; he intends to violate our covenant and cause us to return empty-handed.
We should now go to the Great Lotus and demand payment from him."
Having seen the king, the messenger returned and was ordered to resume the collection as before.
When the prince returned, he encountered this same messenger once more, who continued to demand payment without ceasing.
The prince said to him, "I have already dispatched [the funds]; how can you still remain here?"
"If you immediately return and do good, it will be well; if you do not leave, severe punishment shall surely be added.
The people, filled with fear, led one another back together. Upon arriving at the kingdom, they reported in detail to the King, saying:
"That Prince Bimbisāra is a man of fierce violence; he violates oaths and betrays his word, refusing to accept our summons and levies. We pray that Your Majesty will quickly devise a prior strategy."
"If it were not so, I fear it would bring about future calamity.
At that time, the king replied to the envoy with a verse:
"When trees are still in their sprouts, even a fingernail can sever them."
"Spreading wide and massive as a great embrace, even axes cannot destroy it.
At that time, King Aṅga was greatly incensed and dispatched a messenger with a letter to King Mahāpadma, saying:
"Bimbisāra has rebelled against my command; bind his neck and send him here."
"If it be not so, I shall go there myself to slaughter them.
You must understand my intent.
Having heard this, King Padma and his ministers were struck with fear, fearing nothing less than the ruin of their kingdom.
He then summoned Bimbisāra, reproaching him for his refusal, and sent a letter along with the messenger.
Bimbisāra replied, "He is a Kṣatriya consecrated king, and I am likewise a Kṣatriya consecrated king; our realms are distinct. For what reason should I pay tribute?"
"I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me the fourfold army so that we may confront one another in battle.
King Padma then reflected within himself and realized that Bimbisāra was capable of accomplishing great deeds; he subsequently sent a reply to King Aṅga, saying:
"I have received your letter regarding the pursuit of Bimbisāra, and you further command that his neck be bound and that he be driven here as a prisoner."
"However, as for this son of mine, I wish him to succeed the former king; though you have issued stern commands, I have not yet dared to comply with them.
If Your Majesty must indeed employ force to suppress us and rely on fierce spirit to overwhelm us, stationing troops across the wilds, I know only to await my punishment."
Upon receiving this memorial, Aṅga was seized with extraordinary rage and immediately issued an edict to mobilize the troops of the entire kingdom and sharpen his weapons, declaring:
"I shall go in person to destroy Padmaka and execute King Śrīghoṣa."

Thereupon, he mobilized tens of thousands of men and thousands of troops; the cavalry and infantry surged forward, banners and standards covered the earth, and the sound of bells and drums deafened the heavens as they marched straight into the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, King Padma-mahābhaya immediately summoned Bimbisāra and entrusted him with the fourfold army.
Having received the king’s command, the prince led the sons of the great ministers and issued this proclamation:
"Aṅga has been our country's long-standing enemy; I shall now take revenge. As the invaders have entered our borders, we await your excellent counsel."
"You all have accumulated merit over many lifetimes and have received the sovereign's favor and grace; by what means can you assist me in defeating the rebels and bringing peace to the people?
They replied, "Although we possess no strategic plans, we dare to exert our utmost strength as your limbs to serve as attendants to the Crown Prince."
At that time, Bimbisāra spoke these verses:
"Ruling the kingdom and nourishing the common people, one ought to protect them well;
if they are plundered by others, the myriad subjects lose their refuge."
At that time, the Prince addressed the people, saying, "All of you,
with one heart and united strength, protect me. Having spoken these words,
he issued orders to the three armies, and the troops and horses all set forth.
At that time, King Mahāpadma ascended a high tower and, surrounded by his attendants in front and behind, surveyed the army and said to his ministers,
"Whose troops are these?"
He replied, "This is the army of Prince Bimbisāra. The king said:
"You should know that this army is exceedingly vast;
it should be called 'Shadow-Conquering Army' (Bimbisāra).
Some among them praised the prince's majestic power and magnificent marks in various ways, calling him "Great Ladder Shadow-Conquering" (Mahānirghoṣa-Bimbisāra), and so forth.
At that time, the Prince addressed the people, saying:
"I have heard that a skilled warrior does not weary his army in battle.
Now King Aṅga possesses a great host of troops, their number being exceedingly vast; it would be improper to clash with them and cause injury to my own forces."
"In strategic maneuvers and secret decisions, capturing the enemy is the priority.
He immediately recruited brave warriors and, waiting for them to be unprepared, killed Aṅga.
The three armies and six divisions dispersed all at once; thereupon, he marshaled his troops and pursued the retreating foe, pressing forward against them.
The people of that country, unaware of the king’s death, remained securely stationed within their fortified city.
At that time, Prince Bimbisāra immediately had the king’s head impaled on a spear and displayed it inside the city, then issued a proclamation, saying:
“This is the head of your country’s King Aṅga; you should open the gates at once.”
"If you do not do so, we shall lose our lives at the same time.

Hearing this, the multitude was struck with great terror and immediately opened the gates; all the high ministers bound their necks in submission, and among the common people, there was none who did not submit.
At that time, after Prince Bimbisāra had entered the city, he dispatched a messenger to report back to his father, the King, saying:

"By the majesty of Your Majesty and the diligent efforts of your subjects, the rebel Aṅga has now been executed; the entire realm is free from peril, with peace prevailing afar and order restored near."
Having heard this, Padmā was filled with immeasurable joy; she immediately sent various garments, necklaces, ornaments for the body, and a parasol made of the seven precious gems to Bimbisāra.
Even if he were to appoint Campā as king to succeed Aṅga, the people of that country would collectively call him Mahārāja Bimbisāra.
Later, his sagely virtue and divine merit would pervade both the hidden and the manifest;
the populace would enjoy abundance and joy, bandits and rebels would be eliminated, and his majestic virtue and glorious reputation would spread far and wide.
Later, at another time, King Padma passed away. The ministers and officials of the kingdom of Magadha sent word of their grief and requested his return to rule over their own country.

At that time, Bimbisāra entrusted the affairs of the kingdom of Campā to those former ministers and, having prepared his carriage, traveled with great haste to return to his home country out of mourning.

Once the period of mourning was completed, he succeeded his father as king; he transformed the people through the Dharma, so that the winds were temperate and the rains timely, the hundred grains ripened in abundance, and the myriad subjects enjoyed peace once more.
As his virtue became ever more exalted, neighboring states admired his transformative influence, and there were no longer any enemies or bandits.
At that time, there was a son of a Brahmin in the Central Kingdom who, wishing to study magical arts, traveled everywhere until he gradually reached the South.
In South India, there was a great Brahmin named Diśācārya who was well-versed in the four treatises and was known in the world as the Great Master.
[The youth] immediately went to that master’s place, prostrated at his feet, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
"I pay my respects to you, Master, as your disciple."
He then asked: "What do you wish to study? He replied:
"I am now studying the Great Treatise on the Four Vidyās.
The Master said,
"Study whatever you wish."
He then proceeded to study all manner of worldly arts and the Brahminical rites.
According to the Brahminical law, on the third day of every month, he performed no activities whatsoever; at times he would bathe, or enter the city, or burn wood in the fire.
When the day arrived, the sons of the brahmins went together to fetch wood for cremation, proceeding along the road.
As they went, they asked one another about their lineages and places of birth; each of the four castes, including the Vatsa, spoke according to his own status.
They further questioned one another,
saying, "From which direction do you come? One then replied:
"I am the East," some might say; "I am the South," others might say.
Some said, "I am from the West. Others said:
"I am from the north," he said, adding further:
"I have seen and heard of all those lands."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Wisdom arises in the eastern direction; Slander dwells in the western land;
Respectful compliance is born in the southern land; Harsh speech resides in the northern direction."
The sons of the brahmins spoke thus:
"We know all other regions, but we do not know what it is like in the Middle Country.
The disciples then consulted their teacher, saying:
“Upādhyāya! I now wish to go to the Middle Country to see that land, and furthermore, I wish to bathe in its waters and pay my respects to the various masters of that region.”
"We wish to defeat that master of treatises in that country; our fame will surely be heard far and wide, and we shall obtain much precious wealth for our benefit."
That brahmin felt great affection for his disciples; he distributed all his clothing and belongings among them, and once their provisions were prepared, they set out together for the Middle Kingdom.

As he traveled along the road, whenever other wise men encountered him, he would debate with them and always emerge victorious; some were so impressed that they submitted to him, pouring ashes from jars over their own heads as a sign of submission;
others came to learn from him the arts of horsemanship, archery, and weaponry, all of which he taught them;
and still others came to welcome him, carrying incense, flowers, banners, pennants, and precious parasols.
Furthermore, immeasurable numbers of people all came to him and served him as their teacher.
As he gradually traveled through various countries, he achieved victory over every city, town, and village until he finally reached the Middle Kingdom.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"I have heard that all those who possess wisdom reside at the king's gate.
We should also go there today and subdue him; how might we do so?"

It is like a great tree with its roots and branches and leaves; those places where I have gone and prevailed in debate are like the branches and leaves, but to prevail before the king is like striking at the root. I should now go to the king’s presence.
He then departed immediately.
Upon reaching the king's location, he offered this blessing:
"May you enjoy long life, free from all calamities and obstacles."
Standing to one side, he addressed the king, saying:
"I have received a small measure of learning from my teacher; I wish to engage in a discussion with the teachers within Your Majesty’s realm."
The king then said, "Do as you please.
The king further addressed his ministers, saying:
"In this kingdom of mine, is there such a Brahmin who can debate with that man?
The ministers replied, "There is a Brahmin in the village of Nāla who understands the four Vedas; his wisdom is like fire."
"He himself composed this treatise and titled it 'Māṭhara.
The King said, "Summon his upādhyāya here."
The minister, following these instructions, invited him to the king’s presence,
where he offered the same benediction as before. The king then said, “Are you able to debate with that brahmin before me?”
He replied, "Accepting Your Majesty’s command, I shall dare to respond with all my strength and ability.
He immediately constructed a maṇḍala according to the ritual rules and prepared seats on both sides.
The king then issued a command, saying,
"Who shall be given first?
The ministers replied:
"A guest brahmin named Bhūmika should be allowed to go first.
Having been granted the priority, he recited five hundred verses and then remained silent.
At that time, Māṭhara recited his verses from memory, but they contained many errors;
he then remarked, "The meaning of what you have recited is highly inconsistent and does not accord with reason."
Upon hearing this, the master of the earth remained silent and said nothing.
According to the rules of debate, to remain silent and fail to respond constitutes defeat.
The king said to his ministers:
"Who has been victorious?
Who has been defeated?"
The minister replied, "Māṭhara has won the debate.
The king was pleased in his heart and spoke these words:
“Within my kingdom, there is likewise a person of such intelligence and great wisdom.
The King asked,
“In which village does the Upādhyāya reside?”
He replied, “The village of Nāla.
The king immediately bestowed a reward upon him.
"The village of Nala is at your disposal for your enjoyment.
It is the common custom of the world that all people desire happiness.
There were certain Brahmin women who had been seeking husbands but had not yet succeeded in finding one.
At that time, Māṭhara took a wife from among his own kind, and they lived together in joy and pleasure.
Before long, a son was born, for whom he held an extensive celebration.
Because the boy’s body was tall, he gave him the name Dīrgha (Long Body).

He was nurtured and raised with various provisions until he gradually grew up; he was taught the arts and crafts, namely: calculation, hand gestures (*mudrā*), the practices of a Brahmin, ritual purification, the taking of ashes and earth, the recitation of praises for the four Vedas, and the performance of sacrifices and the study of their recitation—thus mastering all six types of duties.
At a later time, another daughter was born, whose eyes were like those of a maina bird.
When her relatives gathered together, they established a name for her, calling her Mainā.
The girl was raised and nurtured until she gradually grew up; her father then taught her the methods of writing and philosophical debate.
Later, on another occasion, she engaged in debate with her brother, challenging and refuting one another.
When his sister won, the father said to his son:
"You are a man, yet you have been defeated in debate by a woman.
If I am to have no heir, all my possessions will surely be lost to others."
Later, in the land of South India, there was a Brahmin youth named Tiṣya who was highly proficient in the doctrine of no future life.
Seeking the Dharma, he traveled from the south to the abode of Māṭhara; having prostrated at his feet, he addressed him, saying:
"Great Master!..."
"I wish to study under my upādhyāya.
He asked, "What art do you wish to learn?"
He said, "I wish to study the doctrine that there is no future life. He replied:
"Do as you wish. Having received the teaching, when it was time for him to leave and study, the matters discussed were as previously explained in detail.
Later, the youth Tiṣya debated with his teacher before the King, each establishing two propositions.
"This Māṭhara is the most senior in years; he should be questioned first.
Thereupon, the Māṭhara thought to himself:
"That son of a brāhmaṇa has newly completed his studies in logic; I fear he will be difficult to defeat. Now, I must seize upon his errors."
Having formed this thought, Māṭhara immediately recited five hundred verses first.
When that son of a brahmin had finished responding in verse, Māṭhara seized upon his faults, saying:
"This is incoherent speech; these words are illogical; this exposition is unacceptable."
He then remained silent. Generally, when one fails in debate and has no words with which to respond, this constitutes a defeat.
At that time, the king asked his ministers:
"Who has won this?
The minister addressed the king,
saying, "The brahmin Tiṣya has won."
Then the king declared,
"The victor shall be granted a village.
At that time, the ministers came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"If he comes to debate and achieves victory, we shall grant him a village; thus, the kingdom of Magadha will soon be entirely exhausted.
We should take the village of Mataṅga and give it to him for his use."
The king then replied,
"So be it," and immediately confiscated the lands granted for the use of Māṭhara, bestowing them instead upon Tiṣya.
The māṭhara then commanded his wife, saying: "O fair-faced one!
You should quickly prepare our belongings and go to another region."
His wife asked, "For what reason?
At that time, her husband replied:
"I have served the king for a long time, yet at this time of debate he does not protect me, but has seized my villages and towns.
His wife prepared her belongings, intending to depart.
When the kinsmen heard of this matter, they immediately came and asked,
"Upādhyāya! For what reason have you prepared yourself for travel?"
He replied, "I have served the king for a long time, yet when we engaged in debate, he did not protect me; therefore, I have departed.
His kinsmen reported this.
"This dwelling is excellent; among our kinsmen, we request that you stay here.
He then spoke in verse:
"Having been deceived by others in my own land, Dwelling in a foreign land is most excellent."
"The place where one is not deceived is one's own native land and kinsmen.
Having heard this, the brahmin Tiṣya replied, "Upādhyāya!"
"I am but a guest; having stayed for a short while, I shall depart.
You may enjoy the use of this village, and I shall return it to you.
At that time, although Moṭṭarā had received such kindness, he still refused to remain.
Tiṣya spoke again:
"You should stay here for now; let us divide the town, and I shall take half. He replied:
"Excellent! Māṭhara then commanded his wife, saying,
"O fair-faced one!
"For a long time I have served the king, yet he did not protect me; now Tiṣya has shown me the greatest kindness by granting me half a city.
I shall give this daughter of mine to him as his wife."
The wife said,
"Wait for the eldest son, Kuśadhara.
Her father then commanded his son:
“I have served the King for a long time, yet he was unable to protect me during this debate.
This brahmin Tiṣya has shown great kindness, granting me half a village.”
"Now I am giving Śāri to be his wife.
The son said to his father, "This Tiṣya is our father's enemy; he seized our village and departed. How can it be right for us to become kin with him?"
The father replied, "You are foolish and lack understanding.
Since the parents were firm in their resolve, the son did not dare to disobey; he immediately followed the rites and customs and gave his daughter in marriage to Tiṣya.
At that time, Kuśīla thought to himself:
"I have been deceived today solely because my learning is meager and my knowledge is scant.
However, since this brahmin Tiṣya has gained the victory by explaining the doctrine of no future world, I too should study it."
Having formed this thought, he immediately asked:
"In which region or country do you people clearly understand the doctrine that there is no future life? Someone replied:
"The South is the best.
He then traveled by stages until he reached Southern India, where he inquired throughout the country:
"Who understands the doctrine that there is no future life?"
Someone replied, "A certain brahmin. Having heard this,
he immediately went to the brahmin's location and said:
“Venerable sir, I wish to serve you as my teacher; I pray that you will compassionately accept me.
The teacher then asked: “What do you seek?”
He replied, "I wish to study the doctrine that there is no future life.
The brahmin responded:
"I do not instruct lay householders.
He replied, "If that is so,
I shall now go forth into homelessness."
The brahmin immediately granted him ordination, whereupon he made a solemn vow:
"If I do not master this doctrine, I shall never clip my nails.
As his nails grew longer and longer, the people of the time all called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).
At that time, Śāriputra and the brahmin Tiṣya enjoyed themselves in sensual pleasures.

Then there was a pure deva who had long planted roots of goodness and was destined for his final body; he took no delight in birth and death, seeking exclusively nirvāṇa and not seeking further existence.
Bearing his final body, he passed away from the Pure Heaven and was conceived within the womb of Śarī.
At the moment of conception, his mother dreamed that a person holding a torch entered her belly;
she further dreamed that she ascended a great mountain and soared into the void.
Furthermore, he saw the great assembly prostrating before his own body.
When Śāriputra awoke from the dream, he immediately recounted these dreams to his husband.
Although that Brahmin Tiṣya was learned in the manuals of dream interpretation, he was not conversant with this particular matter.
He immediately went to a Brahmin who was well-versed in the interpretation of dreams and said,
"My wife had such a dream last night. The Brahmin replied:
"This dream is most auspicious," the Brahmin predicted. "A virtuous son shall be born who,
at the age of fourteen, will be able to recite the treatises of Śakra and others with great skill."
Furthermore, he shall become preeminent in all debates, inquiries, and responses.
As for what was said regarding ascending the great mountain, leaping through the void, and being honored by the multitude, these shall come to pass upon his renunciation of the world.
“He possesses great majestic power, has accomplished the Great Precepts, and is revered by gods and humans.
Having made this prediction, at a later time, the brahmin Tiṣya engaged Śāriputra in debate, and Śāriputra emerged victorious.
At that time, Tiṣya thought to himself:
"In the past, when we debated, I was victorious;
yet now I am not his equal—what could be the cause for this?"
He further thought to himself:
"This must have been due to the womb; it is his majestic power.

Then, at a later time, when ten months were complete, a boy was born, whose appearance was dignified and handsome, endowed with perfect physical marks. His body was the color of purple gold; his head was as round as a parasol; his hands reached below his knees; his forehead was broad and even; and his nose was high and straight—described in detail as in other accounts.
When his kinsmen had assembled and wished to bestow a name upon him, they asked, "What name should we give him?
The father said, "This child should be taken to his maternal grandfather; he shall bestow a name."
Having arrived at the old man’s place, he said to him, “Great Elder!
What name should be given to this son?”
The father said, "Since he is the son of Tiṣya, it is fitting that his name be Upatiṣya.
The messenger took the child back, and Tiṣya asked:
"What name shall you give him?
He replied, "I shall name him Upatiṣya."
At that time, Tiṣya thought to himself:
"Since this child has already been given a name according to his paternal lineage, I shall now give him a designation according to his maternal lineage, naming him Śāriputra."
At that time, some people called him Śāriputra and others called him Upatiṣya.
He was entrusted to eight nurses.
These mothers raised him, providing him with the finest milk, curd, and clarified butter; he grew up rapidly, like a lotus emerging from the water.
As he gradually grew up, he was instructed to pursue his studies; he attained complete mastery of all worldly arts and crafts, and the four Vedas were fully retained within his mind.
By the age of sixteen, he had excellently understood the Śabdavidyā (science of grammar) of Indra and was able to refute the arguments of others.
Later, at another time, he recited the Vedas and other treatises before his father, and the son said to his father:
"What is the meaning and purport of what I have just recited?"
The father said, "I do not know now. He replied:
"What we recite here is a hymn composed by the seers of antiquity.
Although people of the present age do not understand its meaning, it is not without principle that the seers offered such praise."
As for Śāriputra, since his learning surpassed that of all others, his father’s five hundred disciples who had previously been under his tutelage all returned to Śāriputra.
At that time, Śāriputra instructed his disciples in all the śāstras and sciences, leaving nothing unmastered.
At that time, in the village of Vanavāsin, there lived a great minister named Chāyā, who was very wealthy, possessed of vast riches, and enjoyed abundant prosperity.

Although he had been married for a long time, he had no offspring at all; constantly longing for a son, he prayed everywhere, making petitions to all the mountain deities and tree spirits of the forests—thus it is told in detail.
At that time, a person in their final birth passed away from the heavens and entered his mother’s womb; the details are as explained above.
Once the child was born, a grand gathering of relatives was held, and they wished to bestow a name upon him.
The people replied, "Since he was brought here by the gods holding him, he may be named 'Brought by the Gods' (Devadatta), and he may also be named Maudgalyāyana."

At that time, the elder entrusted the child to eight nurses to raise him. He grew up like a lotus emerging from the water; as it is said at length, he attained complete mastery of the six types of arts and the four Vedas.
At that time, the deity Upatiṣya took five hundred disciples under his tutelage; when their studies were concluded, the five hundred disciples entered the city chanting praises.
Upatiṣya’s other disciples likewise entered the city chanting praises.
At that time, the disciples of Tiṣya replied to the disciples of Maudgalyāyana, saying,
"Venerable sirs, for what reason do you recite the treatise incorrectly? They asked:
“How is that? he asked again.
“Where did you gentlemen study?”
He replied: "My teacher is like the sun and the moon, endowed with all-encompassing wisdom.
In the village of Veṇugrāma, there was a son of a high minister named Maudgalyāyana; it was from him that I studied."
Upatiṣya’s disciple, fully accomplished in learning, free from fear, and filled with joy, immediately went to his preceptor.
When the Master saw him coming, he asked,
"For what reason are you so joyful? He replied:
"There is nothing.
The Master then spoke in verse:
"All internal mental states and emotions should likewise be understood by analogy."
"By means of the faculties of sound, form, and shape, one knows that what is hidden cannot be apprehended.
Having spoken this verse, he said to his disciples:
"There must certainly be something significant here."
At that time, the disciples related the circumstances in detail, and the teacher immediately replied:
"That which he recites is my own reversed text; it is entirely without error."
Having heard this, the disciples remained silent and were not pleased.
At that time, the disciples of Maudgalyāyana went to their teacher’s place; they were all likewise displeased, and when the teacher saw them, he asked:
"Why are you not joyful?"
He replied, “There is nothing. The Master then said:
"There must be a reason for this; why did he not speak?
At that time, the disciple related the circumstances in detail, and the teacher said:
"As for what he recited, his preceptor was indeed brilliant and wise; whether it be long discourses or short discourses, concise texts or extensive citations, they were all exceedingly skillful."
At that time, the two teachers, having heard of one another, desired to meet.
Then Upatiṣya went to his father’s place and said,
"I wish to go for a short while to the village of Venuvana."
The father asked,
"For what reason? He replied:
"He has a minister named Chāyā, who has a son named Kūṭadanta; I wish to meet him.
The father said, "That man’s wisdom surpasses yours."
The son replied to his father, "In terms of wisdom we are not surpassed; however, he possesses great wealth and many riches, and is praised by all.
Then Upatiṣya spoke this verse:
"The aged are to be honored; those with great wealth are also honored;
but one who possesses much learning is honored and served by all.
When the father heard his son's words, he said to him:
"If he comes here, we may instruct him; we should not go to him.
Then Kuruta went to his father and said, "I wish to go to the village of Nalada."
The father asked,
"For what reason?
The son replied to his father:
"There is a brahmin named Tiṣya who has a son named Upatiṣya; I wish to go and meet them.
The father said to his son, "He is wealthier than you."
The son said, "It is not that he is wealthier than I; rather, it is because his wisdom surpasses mine.
Then Kūṭadanta spoke this verse:
"The aged are to be honored; those of great learning are also honored;
and those who possess much wealth are all likewise honored and served.
The father said to his son:
"If he should come here, you should give him wealth and goods; you should not go to meet him.
Later, at another time, there was a great festival in the city of Rājagṛha.
It was the king’s established custom to either go in person or dispatch the crown prince.
On this occasion, the king had other business and could not go himself; he therefore sent the crown prince Ajātaśatru to leave the city for recreation.
At that time, upon hearing that the Crown Prince had gone out on an excursion, Kāla the Shadow conceived this thought:
"When King Bimbisāra dies, the unborn prince shall succeed to the royal throne, and I, Kāla, shall serve him as his minister."
Having formed this thought, he addressed his son, saying:
"You should go to that place of recreation and arrange four high seats, namely:
the King’s seat, the Minister’s seat, the Seat of Sound, and the Brahmin’s seat."
He further told his son,
"You should take a seat upon the high seat of the great minister.
Having heard his father's words, he immediately went there and sat down.
At that time, Tiṣya also heard that King Bimbisāra had sent the crown prince out of the city for recreation.

He immediately told his son: "You should go there and inspect the four high seats. Place your water jar, alms bowl, and mendicant’s staff upon the third seat; you shall sit upon the fourth high seat. No masters of debate, from sunrise until sunset, are your equal."
Having heard this, the son followed the instructions and went to take his seat.
At that time, while the people performed various kinds of music, singing, and praises, Upatiṣya remained silent.
When the people saw this, they said to one another, "This man must surely be either greatly foolish or possessed of great wisdom; that is why he remains silent.
At that moment, all the musicians ceased their performance.
At that time, Kullūta asked Upatiṣya,
"Do you see those musicians and singers? He replied:
"I have composed my internal contemplation and do not see this matter.
He replied, "If you do not see it, can you not at least hear it?"
Upatiṣya replied with a verse:
"Dead skin and sinews produce music, Causing the multitude to feel joy;
But impermanence is as swift as a wheel— The wise know it is not true happiness."
When Kṛṣṇa and the assembly had heard these verses, they immediately asked, "Are you Upatiṣya? He replied:
"O Great Assembly, you should know!
I am Upatiṣya. He then asked Kuḷidatta:
“Did you see the music and other such things as described above? He replied, “I did not.”
Again he replied: "You are so absorbed in internal contemplation that you cannot even hear with your ears.
Then Kṛmilā answered him in verse:
"All these various ornaments, which adorn the body and bring it heavy burden, and the dancing that moves the physical frame—all are comprised within the category of falsehood.
Those who sing and perform plays are like the sound of shouting; all such things are impermanent—reflect on this, for what joy is there in them?"
At that time, Upatiṣya asked, "Are you Kūṭadanta?
and the people replied:
"So be it," Upatiṣya replied. "I have come for your sake; let us go forth together."

Kṛtaka replied: "The various sacrifices performed, the offerings made to the fire god, and the ascetic practices undertaken to seek merit—the fruits and retributions of all these are now in your hands."
"My family is of the ministerial caste; I have always ridden upon elephants—why should I go forth into homelessness?
At that time, Upatiṣya spoke this verse:
"When a tree is about to fall, its branches and leaves cannot support one another."
"At the time of death it shall be just so; one's enjoyments cannot provide salvation. Having spoken this verse, Upatiṣya said: "Come, sir!"
"Let us go forth together.
He replied, "I shall ask my parents."
He said, "Go, my son. When he had spoken thus, Kūṭadanta went at once to his father’s presence and said:
"Father, please release me so that I may leave the household life with pure faith and go forth from home.
His father replied, "The various sacrifices you have performed,
the rites for worshipping the fire god, and the fruits of the ascetic practices you sought— all these you have now obtained."
"Furthermore, you are the son of a high minister and a rider of elephants; you ought to serve as a high minister—why have you renounced the world?
At that time, Kūṭadanta spoke a verse before his father:

"Better to wear garments of tree bark in the forest, Dwelling among the beasts and eating various fruits; Than to dwell in a palace with a hundred courtesans, And yet remain bound by the fetters of desire."
"One does not imprison or bind others for matters of state; the wise do not engage in acts that cause fear.
Having heard this verse, the father said:
"You are my only son, like the crescent moon; I love you as I have described at length before."
"Every son must rely upon his parents; since your resolve is unwavering, you may follow me and leave the household life.

Having received this permission, his companions all arrived together. At that time, Kṛṣṇa (Kullipa) immediately gave rise to a superior mind, exerting himself in body and spirit, and set out for the village of Nālada.
That Upatiṣya constantly delighted in tranquility; dwelling in an araṇya, he led five hundred disciples and had them recite the Brahmaviśeṣacinti Brāhmaṇa mantra.
Then Kūṭadanta proceeded by stages until he reached the village of Nālada,
where he asked the people, "Where is Upatiṣya now?"
The villagers replied, "He is currently at the āraṇya, leading a community of five hundred, reciting the Brahma-śānti mantra.
Thereupon, Kūṭadanta went to the āraṇya; having met him, he addressed Upatiṣya as follows:
"The time has now come for the life of a renunciant.
Upatiṣya asked, "Has your father given you permission to go forth?"
He replied, "I have. Upatiṣya said to Kolita:
“Virtuous one, please stay for a moment while I also ask my father whether he will allow me to go forth.
Kṛtaka said, “If you go now to ask him, when will you be able to return?”
He replied, "I shall go for a moment and return immediately.
Upatiṣya went to his parents' place and said to them:
"I now have a request; I pray you will show me compassion. It is my wish to seek pure renunciation.
His parents replied, "This is most excellent; we grant your wish and allow you to renounce the world."
Then Upatiṣya returned to the place where Kolita was and said to him: "Kolita!
My parents have given their permission; come, let us go forth together."
He asked again:
"O people! Have your parents given you permission to leave the household life?"
The crowd replied, "We have granted permission. Then Kūṭadanta said:
"I have been questioning my parents for many days; what plan have you devised that you return so quickly?
He replied, "The karmic conditions of your family are heavy and firmly bound, which is why I was delayed."
My family’s affairs are few and light; therefore, I have come early.
Not only today, but throughout five hundred lifetimes, I have already left the household life.
Furthermore, I have constantly made this vow: "May I be born neither in a noble nor a lowly station, but be born into the middle class."
"Because my bonds are light due to this, I have come so swiftly.
Then Kūṭadanta said to the crowd: "My lineage is noble;
now that I wish to renounce the world, how could I do so in a haphazard manner?"
"Let us go together to the royal city and question those pure brahmins.
At that time, the six heretical teachers were in that city, each of whom claimed to have attained supernatural powers, mastery, and unimpededness.
Then Upatiṣya, Kolita, and the others asked the six teachers, beginning with Pūraṇa Kāśyapa:
"What Dharma-eye do you practice?
What teachings do you study?"
"What further fruit is obtained?
If one maintains the holy life, what extraordinary excellence is attained?
His teacher replied:
"I see thus, I declare thus: 'There is no giving, no sacrifice, no offering;
there is no fruit or ripening of good or evil deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no father, no mother, and no spontaneously born beings;

in this world there are no arhats who have practiced rightly and attained right accomplishment, who, having realized this world and the next through their own superknowledge, have declared their perfection.'"
Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.
Having experienced only this life, I have severed future becoming; at the end of my life, I shall utterly pass away.
The four great elements combine to form what is conventionally designated as a human body.
When this life is severed, the four elements each return to their original places, and the fifth element, space, remains.

The sense faculties then cease to function; this corpse is taken to the forest and cremated. Once it has turned to ash and the skeletal remains have become the color of pigeons, there is no person at all.

Having thus attained realization, one knows that for the wise, both the giver of a gift and the recipient of a gift—those who speak of "existence"—are all empty and false assertions, mere hollow cries, and nothing but the talk of fools.
"If one is a wise person, they understand that both are subject to cessation and destruction, and thus know there is no future body.
At that time, Kūṭadanta and Upatiṣya thought to themselves:
"This teacher dwells in a non-path and practices what is not wisdom; you, O virtuous one, should not follow him to study and practice such a perilous path."
He spoke in verse: "Misunderstanding is not a good teaching; one’s mind delights in inferior dharmas.
If such is the case with the well-taught Dharma, what need is there to speak of that which is not the Dharma?"
Having spoken these words, you should know that he was like one striking an empty vessel; having struck it, he departed.
Next, he went to the place of Makkhali Gosāla and said:
"Venerable sir, what is the eye of the Dharma that you practice?"
What teachings have you practiced?
What fruit have you attained?
And what extraordinary excellence is gained by maintaining the holy life?
He replied: "I speak thus and see thus: there is no cause and no condition."
Sentient beings undergo suffering without cause or condition; they attain purity not by means of causes and conditions, but naturally attain purity without cause or condition.
Sentient beings lack wisdom and vision; yet, without cause or condition, sentient beings naturally possess wisdom and vision.
There is no power, no diligence, no man, no worldly force, no self-form, no other-form, no action by self, and no action by another.
All sentient beings, all living creatures, and all categories of existence have no fixed location, no dwelling place, and no objective locus.
They take refuge in the definitive right path, awakening to the experience of suffering and pleasure—namely, the sentient beings of the six realms.
Then Kūṭadanta and Upatiṣya thought to themselves:
"This teacher dwells on a non-path and rides upon a wrong path; the wise avoid him, for this is a perilous road."
Having understood this, he spoke these verses:
"Those with wrong understanding do not speak well; Their hearts delight in inferior dharmas.
If the True Dharma is such as this, What then can be said of what is not the Dharma?"
Having spoken these words, he realized that [the teacher] was like one striking an empty vessel;
knowing him to be no [true teacher], he departed. Next, he went to the place of Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra and said:
"Venerable sir, what is the eye of the Dharma you practice?"
What teachings did he practice?
What fruit did he attain?
And what was his excellence?
"What brahmacarya do you practice? He replied, "Māṇava!"
In this regard, I hold such a view and speak thus:
"You should act in this way for the sake of taking life; you should do so yourself, and you should also instruct others to do so."
One should set oneself on fire, as well as command others to burn, cut, hack, or harm;
one should likewise act in such ways, take what is not given, engage in sexual desire, speak falsehoods, and drink alcohol and the like.
Even if one were to pile up mountains of people and kill them with sharp blades, or mince them into heaps,
there would be no sinful karma from such various acts of killing, nor would there be any retribution.

On the southern bank of the Ganges, various forms of killing are practiced; on the northern bank, various assemblies for sacrificial offerings are established. [They claim] there is neither sin nor merit.

Yet, if one practices such dharmas as giving, ethical discipline, and diligence, as well as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one will obtain a great fruit of retribution even if one does not perform those [sacrifices].
At that time, Kūṭadanta and Upatiṣya said to one another: "This teaching is irrational;
it is entirely a false doctrine. One should be terrified of it; the wise should stay far away from it."
Having spoken these words, he recited this verse:
"Wrong understanding is not well-spoken; The mind delights in inferior dharmas.
If even the True Dharma is thus, How much more so that which is not the Dharma?"
Having spoken these words, he departed, leaving him like one who has struck an empty vessel.
He then went to the place of Ajita Keśakambalin and said:
"Virtuous sir, what is the eye of the Dharma that you practice?"
What instruction did he give?
What was his excellence?
What holy life did he practice?
"What further fruit do you obtain? He replied, "O Māṇava!"
I hold such a view and speak thus:
there are furthermore seven bodies. What are the seven?

That which is called earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life—all these are without agency and without that which is acted upon; they are without transformation and without that which is transformed; they are without harm, yet they abide as an accumulation, just as the branches of a tree support one another. They are all unarisen because they are subject to no change, and thus they reach a state where they do not injure one another.

Whether it be merit or demerit, or by means of merit and demerit; whether it be suffering or pleasure, or by means of suffering and pleasure—among these seven, who is the person capable of killing another?
Both the slayer and the slain lack any sovereign master; thus, they do not destroy the world.

Life resides within the six constituents, dwelling in the orifices and acting as their lord; it is ultimately beyond harm, and therein neither is there any who can inflict injury, nor is there any strife.

There is no one who awakens, nor is there any act of awakening; there is no recollection, no one who reflects, no one who expresses, and no one who indicates. These constitute the primary gateway among the fourteen thousand six hundred gateways of departure for liberation.
Furthermore, there are five types of karma:
three are to be performed (*kārya*) and two are what has been performed (*kṛta*); there are also complete karmas and partial karmas.
There are sixty-four thousand subordinate observations (*vyūha*), sixty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), and one hundred and thirty *nāraka* sense-faculties (*indriya*).

Furthermore, there are one hundred and thirty-six realms of disease, forty-nine thousand dragon retinues, forty-nine thousand garuḍas, forty-nine thousand retinues of Nirgranthas, and forty-nine thousand retinues of non-Buddhist outsiders.

There are seven eons of existence, seven eons of non-existence, seven worlds of asuras, seven worlds of piśācas, seven celestial abodes, seven human realms, seven great lakes, seven small lakes, seven great dreams, seven hundred minor dreams, seven great precipices, seven hundred minor precipices, seven great awakenings, and seven hundred minor awakenings; there are six births of exquisite beauty and ten increases by way of a mahāpuruṣa.

These are eighty-four thousand great kalpas; within them, there is no fool or wise person who does not undergo transmigration before finally attaining the exhaustion of suffering and only then achieving liberation.
For example, if a heavy object wrapped with thread is thrown down from a height, it will spin until the thread is exhausted.
It is the same for both the foolish and the wise: after wandering through birth and death for eighty-four thousand kalpas, they attain liberation at the end of those kalpas.
Among them, if any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas can speak thus:
"By means of these precepts, I diligently practice the holy life;
those who are not yet matured, I shall cause to reach maturity."
‘As for those who have reached maturity, they will exhaust their suffering and obtain the fruit’— to speak thus is impossible. Rather,
suffering and pleasure abide as they are, without increase or decrease, and cannot be known [otherwise].”
"I have spoken thus:
'To fully understand birth and death is the truth, not falsehood.
When he had said this, Kūṭadanta and Upatiṣya both thought to themselves:
"However, this teacher dwells upon a non-path, like a treacherous road; the wise should keep far away from him.
Having thought thus, he spoke these verses:
"His understanding is erroneous and his teaching is not virtuous; In his heart, he delights in inferior dharmas."
"Since the True Dharma is thus, how could the non-Dharma be otherwise?
Having spoken this verse, it was as if striking an empty vessel; the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Next, he went to the place of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and said:
"Venerable sir, what is the eye of the Dharma you practice?
What is your teaching?"
What excellence is there?
What is the holy life?
And what fruit is obtained?
He replied: "I see it thus; I speak thus:
all the karmic retributions experienced by sentient beings arise entirely from their past actions."
Past evil karma has been exhausted; by now practicing the holy life, one attains the end of suffering.
Having obtained the fruit through the causes and conditions of present wholesome karma, one no longer creates evil and shall attain the exhaustion of outflows.
"Once the outflows are exhausted, suffering and karma are both exhausted.
When the fruits of suffering are exhausted, one reaches the ultimate limit.
At that time, having heard these words, Kūṭadanta and Upatiṣya thought to themselves:
"This teacher’s doctrine also dwells in a non-path, like a perilous road; the wise should avoid it.
He spoke a verse, saying:
"Wrong understanding is not a good teaching; One's heart delights in inferior dharmas."
"Since the True Dharma is thus, what indeed would the non-Dharma be like?
Having spoken these verses, he departed immediately, just as when striking an empty vessel, as described at length previously.
