Herein is the account of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana crossing over [to the other shore].
At that time, there was a teacher named Sañjayin; [Śāriputra] went to him and asked the people there:
“Where is this teacher sitting in meditative seclusion?
The teacher was already in his room; having heard these words, he thought to himself:
“I have been here for a long time, yet I have never heard such talk regarding meditative seclusion.”
At that time, Kṛtaka and the others thought to themselves:
"That man is sitting in meditation; we should not cause him to rise prematurely. We shall wait until he has finished his sitting and risen, and then we shall meet him."
Having had this thought, he concealed himself in a secluded place.
At that time, Sañjayin rose from his meditative seclusion with his faculties purified.
Knowing this, the two of them went to him and said:
“Virtuous one, what Dharma-eye do you possess?
What instructions do you provide?
What is your excellence?”
"What brahmacarya do you practice?
And what fruit have you attained? He replied:
"I see thus and I speak thus: it is true and not false;
one does not harm living beings; there is no birth and no death, no falling away and no passing out of existence; one shall be reborn among the two Brahmā heavens."
At that time, those two asked:
"What is the meaning of what you have said? He replied:
"One who does not speak falsely is called a renunciant;
one who does not harm living beings takes all dharmas as their root;
that which is eternally without birth or death, without falling or ceasing, and so forth, is Nirvana."
"Those who give birth to the two Brahmās—namely, all those brahmins who practice the holy life (brahmacarya)—all seek that realm.
Having heard these words, he said:
"Venerable One, please accept us and grant us the going forth to practice the holy life."
He immediately granted both men ordination.
Once they had been ordained, the news spread throughout the four quarters that Kṛṣṇa and his companions had received ordination at the site of Saṃśīti.
At that time, Śaṇḍilya acquired great gains and offerings, and he thought to himself:
"In the past, my clan was of the Kauṇḍinya lineage; now, at this time as well, I am of the Kauṇḍinya lineage."
"The profit and sustenance we now receive do not arise from our own merit, but are entirely due to the merit of those two men.
Having had this thought, at that time Śāṇakavāsin, who previously had five hundred disciples whom he constantly taught the treatises, [reflected thus].
He immediately commanded those two to each lead two hundred and fifty disciples and receive his teachings.
At that time, Sanjayin fell ill; then Upatissa said to Kolita:
"The Teacher is now afflicted by illness; shall you seek medicine for him, or shall you attend to him?"
He replied, "Since you possess wisdom, it is fitting that you attend to me; I shall seek out medicine.
At that time, Kūṭadanta obtained various medicinal roots, stalks, flowers, and so forth, which he gave to his teacher to eat and consume, but the illness only grew worse.
At that time, the Teacher smiled, whereupon Tiṣya addressed him, saying:
"A Great Being does not smile without cause.
For what reason has the Teacher now smiled?"
The teacher then said: "It is as you have said.
Regarding what I laughed at previously:
there was a king on Suvarṇadvīpa named Suvarṇapati; when his life came to an end and he was about to be cremated, his wife, overcome with grief and distress, likewise burned her own body."
"Sentient beings are deluded; led by desire and stained by sensual passion, they undergo such suffering. Upatiṣya asked:
"At what year, month, day, and time did such a thing occur?"
He replied, "On such and such a month and day, and at such and such a time.
The two disciples then immediately recorded this.
Again, he said to his teacher:
"The reason I have left the household life is to seek the cessation of birth and death.
Since you, Teacher, have already attained it, I pray that you will now instruct me so that I may also bring an end to birth and death."
The teacher replied:
"It was my intention to leave the household life for the sake of seeking this very thing.
However, as you have requested, I did not attain it."
However, on the fifteenth day during the *poṣadha*, there were hosts of devas in the sky who spoke these words:

"Among the Śākyas, a youth has been born. On the slopes of the Snowy Mountains, there is a river named Vibhaṅga; by its banks is the hermitage of the seer Kapila, where a brahmin resides who is well-versed in celestial astrology and capable of interpreting signs."

He prophesied that the youth shall become a wheel-turning sage king; if he renounces the world, he shall realize the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with his fame heard throughout the ten directions.
He told his disciples:
"When you go forth in that teaching, practice the holy life; you should not rely on the nobility of your lineage, but should instead practice the holy life and subdue your sense faculties."
"You shall obtain wondrous fruits therein and shall not undergo birth and death.
Having spoken these preliminary words, he uttered this verse:
"All that is accumulated must disperse; All that is lofty will inevitably fall."
"Meetings end in separation; all who have life must return to death.

At that time, the Teacher’s life came to an end before long. His disciples wrapped his body in blue, yellow, red, and white silk cloths, carried him to the forest, and after performing the rites, cremated him.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Suvarṇakeśa on the Golden Island who came from there to the city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the place where Upatiṣya was.
Then Upatiṣya asked him, "From where have you come?"
He replied, "I have come from Suvarṇadvīpa.
[The other asked,] "Have you seen any extraordinary things there?"
He replied, “I saw nothing else;
however, when the King, the Lord of Gold, passed away and was cremated, his wife, out of grief and longing for him, also burned herself. He then asked:
"What year, month, day? He replied, "On such-and-such a year,
month, and day, as well as at such-and-such a time."
Upatiṣya then consulted his own private records and found they were indeed as his teacher had said.
At that time, Kolita said to Upatiṣya:
"Our teacher has already realized the sublime Dharma; yet our teacher keeps the secret Dharma and does not teach it to us."
"If the Master had not realized the divine ear and the divine eye, how could he have known that such things exist in other directions?
Then Kūṭadanta thought to himself:
"Upatiṣya is clever and wise; he must have obtained the sublime Dharma from his teacher, yet he does not teach it to me."
Having formed this thought, he immediately said:
"Let us make a solemn vow:
'Whichever of us first realizes the sublime Dharma shall deliver the other.'"
Having made this vow, they traveled together among the people.
At that time, the Bodhisattva was twenty-nine years old and wished to enjoy the pleasures of the five desires within the royal palace.
Having witnessed birth, old age, sickness, and death, he conceived a sense of weary detachment; at midnight, he leaped over the city walls and went to the forest thickets.

After six years of asceticism, having gained nothing at all, he relaxed his breath and began to consume delicious foods such as milk and curd, anointed his body with ghee, and bathed in fragrant water. He then proceeded to the village of Senāni and received from the two cowherd girls, Nandā and Nandabalā, sixteen-fold milk-rice.
After the Bodhisattva had finished eating, the Black Dragon King appeared and praised him, saying, "Excellent!

Then another man named Nitya (Constant Abiding) presented the Bodhisattva with auspicious *kuśa* grass. He then proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree and spread the grass himself; the grass did not become disordered but instead curled to the right. Upon this grass, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), holding his body erect and maintaining right mindfulness, and immediately formed a resolve:
"If my outflows are not exhausted, I shall never rise from this seat.

At that time, although the Bodhisattva had not yet attained realization, he immediately subdued three million six hundred thousand koṭis of evil Māras, each of whom was accompanied by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities.
At that time, having subdued Māra with the armor and weapons of loving-kindness, the Bodhisattva realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, a Brahmā deity came and requested the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma three times in Vārāṇasī.
Among those present in the assembly were more than fifty sons of high ministers; having heard the Dharma, they all requested to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded once again to a village named Śvetavastra-vana.
There were sixty people who were his virtuous companions; having heard the Buddha’s teaching, they immediately attained right faith.
They then proceeded to a village named Senāvatī, where the village head had two daughters:
the first was named Nandā and the second was named Nandabalā. Having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, they likewise attained right faith as before.

Furthermore, there was a lake named Uruvilvā, where a great seer named Kāśyapa resided together with one thousand disciples. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, they all requested to go forth and receive full ordination.
When the Buddha arrived at the Gayāśīrṣa Caitya, he displayed three kinds of miraculous feats before Gayākāśyapa, thereby causing Kāśyapa to abide in the state of parinirvāṇa.
Thereafter, he went to the Śāla Grove and caused King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha, to perceive the Truths.
Together with eighty thousand celestial beings, as well as the brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and stayed in the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Kalandaka Pond in the Bamboo Grove.
Then Upatiṣya and Kolita, while traveling through the countryside, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. Seeing that the city was tranquil, they thought to themselves:
"There are two causes by which this great city dwells in such tranquility:"
"Perhaps there is fear of an enemy;
perhaps it is because of a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa of great majestic power.
Having thought this, he immediately went to observe the stars. Finding no fear of an enemy, he drew three lines on his face and proceeded to travel by stages.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of people following behind him.
Later, at another time, after he had finished adorning his face with makeup and paint, as he wandered along in succession, not a single person followed him. He then thought to himself:
"Previously, when I wandered, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people following me; now there is not a single one. What does this mean?"
At that time, according to the constant custom of all Buddhas as with others, the Buddha immediately formed this thought:
"These followers of heterodox paths—one named Kṣemaka and one named Gārgya—have already planted many roots of goodness and long cultivated meritorious deeds under past Buddhas."
It is like a feverish swelling that, when the season has ripened and it encounters the right conditions, bursts open and is thereby healed.
This person’s faculties have matured; now is precisely the right time.
The Buddha further examined his faculties to determine how he might be delivered and with whom he shared a karmic affinity.

He perceived that this person would develop the aspiration for enlightenment in the presence of one who was fully endowed with the Vinaya discipline; the World-Honored One then commanded the bhikṣu Aśvajit to go there and deliver him.
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit’s deportment was so dignified and orderly that all those among the assembly of devas and humans who saw him were inspired to resolve their minds [for awakening].
The Buddha said to Aśvajit:
“You should accept these two people as your disciples.”
Having received the command, he joyfully remained silent, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately departed.

Then, at the time for the morning meal, Aśvajit put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in sequence, his deportment composed and dignified like that of a bull king.

At that time, the brahmin Upatiṣya went out for a stroll and beheld the Venerable Aśvajit, whose majestic deportment was perfectly complete and rare in the world; he marveled at this unprecedented sight.
At that time, Upatiṣya thought to himself:
"The renunciants in this city are not like these; I should ask them:
'Under whom have you gone forth?'"
"What dharma do you study?
Who is your teacher?
Having had this thought, he went toward a nearby path to wait for the Venerable One.
At that time, the Venerable One arrived from there; having seen him, Upatiṣya immediately asked:
"Who is your teacher? What dharma do you study?"
"Under whom have you gone forth?
Aśvajit replied, "My great teacher is of the Śākya clan, the śramaṇa Gautama; he has now realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"He is my teacher; relying upon him, I have shaved off my hair and beard to go forth as a renunciant, practicing the holy life and reciting the teachings.
At that time, Upatiṣya said: "Venerable one!"
"I pray that you will speak for me, so that I may hear it.
Maṅgala replied, "The teaching of the Tathāgata is extremely profound and subtle; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know."
"I have recently gone forth and am unable to explain it in detail.
However, I cannot now recall the specific words;
I shall briefly state its meaning. Tiṣya replied:
“Please explain its meaning.
Thereupon, Aśvajit addressed him with these verses:
“All phenomena arise from conditions; The Tathāgata has declared their cause;”
"When those dharmas and their causes and conditions are exhausted—this is what the Great Śramaṇa has taught.
Having spoken this verse, Upatiṣya immediately became free from defilement and realized the Dharma-eye, the eye within the Dharma.
Having seen the Dharma, his mind was free from doubt and his heart was devoid of fear; he suddenly rose, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke these words:
"This is my teacher; this is the True Dharma."
Those who abide in this Dharma shall never again fall; it is a state free from sorrow.
Since immeasurable and vast kalpas past, I have never before heard such a profound and essential Dharma.
He then asked the Venerable One:
"Where is the Great Master, the World-Honored One, now? He replied:
"My Great Teacher is at the side of the Kalandaka Pond in Rājagṛha.

Having heard these words, Upatiṣya was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, took his leave, and departed, proceeding immediately to the place where Kolita resided.

At that time, Kuṇḍala saw him approaching from afar and said to Upatiṣya, "Your appearance is now exceptionally radiant and pure, and your faculties are serene; have you attained the supreme Dharma of the Deathless?"
Upatiṣya replied: "So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
Then Upatiṣya related the foregoing matter in detail and spoke this verse:
"All phenomena arise from causes; The Tathāgata has explained their cause.
The cessation of those same phenomena through the exhaustion of their causes— This is what the Great Śramaṇa has taught."
At that time, having heard this Dharma, Kullūta said:
"Venerable One! Speak it for me once more."
Then Upatiṣya repeated it once more:
“The Tathāgata has taught the cause Of all phenomena that arise from conditions;
The cessation of those same phenomena through the exhaustion of their causes Is what the Great Śramaṇa proclaims.”
When this Dharma had been spoken, Kṛṣṇa immediately became free from defilement and realized the Dharma-eye, the eye within the Dharma.
Having seen the Dharma, he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated with joy, and spoke these words:
“This is the True Dharma; those who abide in it shall not fall into the lower realms.”
"From immeasurable koṭis of kalpas ago, I have never heard this Dharma.
Then Kūṭadanta said to Upatiṣya,
"Where is the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, now?"
He replied, "It is at the side of the Kalandaka Pond in Rājagṛha.
Having heard these words, he further addressed Upatiṣya:
"Now it is fitting that we go together to renounce the world there and practice the holy life.
He replied, "Excellent!"
Kṛṣṇa said, "Let us ask our disciples; do they all agree? Upatiṣya replied:
“Excellent, excellent! You are one of renowned virtue, well-known to all; it is fitting that you question the disciples.
Thereupon, Kullūta addressed his disciples, saying:
"I and Upatissa wish now to go to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to leave the household life, study the Way, and practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
What do you think?"
The disciples replied:
"All that we have studied has been according to our teacher's instruction.
Now that our Upādhyāya has followed the Buddha to renounce the household life, we too wish to follow the Buddha and renounce the household life."
The Master said: "Excellent!
Now is precisely the right time."
At that time, Upatiṣya and Kolita, each accompanied by two hundred and fifty disciples, departed from the royal city, intending to go to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove pond.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit was sitting in silent meditation beneath a tree not far from the World-Honored One.
Having seen him from afar, Upatiṣya said to Kolita:
"Should we go first to pay our respects to the World-Honored One?"
"Did you previously listen to the Dharma from your upādhyāya?
Kṛṣṇa replied, "I should have listened to the Dharma at the proper place for hearing the Dharma."
Having spoken these words, they went together to the place where the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin among the assembly who had previously worshipped the moon deity; for that brahmin, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"If a person can understand the Dharma, Whether old or young, it matters not."
"One must arouse reverence, as if toward the newly risen moon.
At that time, there was a fire-worshipping brahmin in the assembly, for whom the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"If a person can understand the Dharma, regardless of whether they are old or young,"
"One must give rise to reverence, for it is like fire that can purify filth.
At that time, Upatiṣya, along with Kolita and the others, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Aśvajit and immediately proceeded to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, who stood before and behind him as he preached the Dharma.
Seeing Kuṇḍadhāna and the others from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Do you see these two men, who stand at the head of the assembly and are surrounded by the great multitude?"
He replied: "It is so! We have already seen it."
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"You should know that these two individuals, having left the household life to study the Path within my Dharma, are the foremost among the śrāvakas in terms of supernormal powers and wisdom."
Then Kullūta and Upatiṣya went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One!”
"We pray that you would grant us ordination and full admission within the sublime Dharma, so that we may become bhikṣus and practice the holy life.
Then the World-Honored One addressed those two men: "Welcome, bhikṣus!"
"Practice the holy life.

Once the Buddha had spoken, the hair and beards of those two men fell away of their own accord, and saffron robes appeared upon their bodies, as if they had been shaved seven days prior; their dignified deportment was perfected like that of bhikṣus of a hundred years' standing. A verse summarizes this:
"At the World-Honored One’s command, 'Come,' their faculties attained tranquility."
With hair fallen off and clad in robes, his majestic deportment was like that of one who had spent a hundred summers [in the monastic life].
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed and taken their bowls at the time of eating, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in succession.
Within that city, the disciples of Sañjayin, upon seeing the bhikṣus, mocked them together and spoke this verse:
“The Buddha, in the city of Rājagṛha, Is the most eminent in Magadha;
Sañjayin has already finished converting all— Who is it now that you intend to convert?”
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they lost their majestic splendor and were not at ease.

Having received almsfood, they returned to their original place; after finishing their meal, they gathered their robes, washed their feet, and went to where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
When we were at our mealtime, begging for alms in the royal city, the disciples of Sañjayin reviled us in various ways. We have related all that occurred above."
"We remain silent, lacking in majestic virtue, and our hearts are unhappy.
The Buddha said,
"If they speak such words, you should answer them thus:"
“Ordination must always be according to the Dharma; the teaching of the World-Honored One is correct.
What do you know that their ordination is in accordance with the Dharma?
When he answered thus, they, lacking in majestic power, departed in silence.
Then the bhikṣus, having put on their robes and taken up their bowls, entered the city of Rājagṛha and went on their alms-round in due order.
At that time, the disciples of Sañjayin reviled them as before, speaking these verses:
“The Buddha is in Rājagṛha, The most excellent in Magadha;”
“Śaṅkha has already been delivered; whom will you deliver now?
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they replied with a verse:
“One who delivers others should do so according to the Dharma; the teaching of the World-Honored One is the correct one.”
"What do you know that he has crossed over by relying on this Dharma?
When the disciples of Sañjayin heard these words, they lost both their majesty and their confidence; they withdrew in silence and dispersed.
Later, at another time, both the Māṭhara brahmin and his wife passed away; the brahmin Tiṣya and his wife Śārī also met their deaths.
Kuśīla returned from the south, bringing the doctrine of the non-existence of future lives to the village of Nālandā.
A gatekeeper asked him,
"Venerable sir!..."
"Are you Kuścidhara? He replied, "It is so."
When the people learned of this,
they asked the gatekeeper, "Where is the brahmin Māṭhara now?"
He replied, "He has already died.
He asked again:
“His wife, Tiṣya, and the others,” he answered in full as before.
He asked again:
“Where is Śāriputra now? He replied, “He is in the city of Rājagṛha.”
"There was a great teacher named Sañjayin who recently appeared in the world; he has gone forth from the household life under him.
Kuśīla then said: "According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, one should not go forth from the household life; this is not a good thing."
Having spoken these words, he traveled by stages until he reached the city of Rājagṛha, where he asked the people,
"Where is the Great Teacher Sañjayin now?"
The people replied, "The Great Master has died.
All his disciples have gone forth as monastics under the śramaṇa Gautama."
He exclaimed: "Excellent! Since he has already made this prediction:"
"He shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), and if he becomes king, Śāriputra should serve as his chief minister.
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin Dīrghanakha went to where the Buddha was and spoke thus: "Śramaṇa Gautama!
Regarding all views concerning the self and phenomena, none are desired by me.
As for those who practice fire-worship and hold such views and make such declarations as:
"That which I have seen is entirely detached from and eliminated by [the truth], and is also free from transformation," [I do not accept this].
"If one is free from this view and does not grasp at continuity, one will no longer grasp at other views.
"O Śramaṇa Gautama! Such is my view; such is my understanding."
What people of the world perceive is for the most part contrary to the practice of fire-worship.
Furthermore, they say that those with such views all abide in this path, O Gautama!
"Do you hold such a view and such an understanding?
Furthermore, the *Kāṣṭhāgnihotra-śāstra* states:
"If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others can abandon this view and not adopt any other view, then these individuals are true śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; this is the subtle and sublime state."
Furthermore, those who serve the sacrificial fire all abide in three views. What are these three?
First, the desire for nothing at all; second, the desire for everything; third, the vow not to desire anything, even unto renouncing the household life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, the bhikṣu Kuśīla is foremost in clear understanding and sharp intelligence."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Then, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did this Śāriputra previously commit?"
"By virtue of that karma, they have attained sharp wisdom, profound wisdom,
and wisdom free from doubt. The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!"
"You all should listen.

Whatever karma Śāriputra previously committed, he must experience its results himself; it does not occur elsewhere," and so on, as extensively explained, up until "the retribution is experienced by oneself."
In the distant past, there was a brahmin in a certain village who, shortly after marrying, gave birth to a son.
Before many years had passed, he fathered a daughter as well; both grew up together.
When his parents fell ill, they both passed away.

Having encountered such grief and sorrow, the youth resolved to go to the mountain forests; he immediately took his younger sister with him to the woods, where they gathered flowers and fruits to sustain themselves.
"O bhikṣus! A great black snake has five defects. What are these five?
First is excessive anger, second is excessive resentment, third is committing evil, fourth is ingratitude, and fifth is a sharp poison.
One should know that women likewise have five faults:
first is excessive anger, second is excessive resentment, third is committing evil, fourth is ingratitude, and fifth is a sharp poison.
What is meant by the "sharp poison" of women?
Generally, all women harbor many fierce and intense desires.
At that time, once the young girl reached maturity, her lustful mind gradually intensified, and she said to her elder brother:
"I can no longer sustain my life by constantly eating fruits and flowers; we should go among the people to seek food and drink.
Thereupon, the elder brother took his sister and together they left the mountain forest, going to the house of a Brahmin to beg for alms.
As they both called out simultaneously, the host came out to look;
seeing them, he remarked, "Does a man living in seclusion also keep a wife?
His elder brother replied:
"This is not my wife; she is my own sister.
He then asked his elder brother, "Have you already betrothed her to someone?"
He replied, "Not yet. [The other] said,
"If that is so, why do you not give it to me?"
He replied, "He has already distanced himself from the unwholesome dharmas of the world.
The woman’s desire was intense, and she said to her brother:
"How could it be that I cannot survive on the fruits and flowers in this forest?
However, being unable to endure the oppression of afflictions, I have left the wilderness with you and traveled far to this human realm; now, you may give me to the brahmin."
The elder brother said, "I truly cannot marry you; this is an evil practice and not something I would do.
You have worldly desires, so act according to your own wishes."
At that time, the brahmin, having understood the woman’s heart, invited her into his home, held a great assembly of his kinsmen, and took her as his wife. He said to her elder brother:
"From now on, she shall live in the same residence as me; let a separate room be prepared for her."
The elder brother said, "I do not seek sensual desires; I shall delight in leaving the household life.
The younger sister said:
"Only after we have established a formal covenant may you act according to your wishes.
The elder brother said,
"What kind of covenant are you speaking of?"
The sister said,
"If you have realized such a sublime fruit, you may come to see me.
The brother said:
"Excellent! It shall be as you have wished.
Having spoken thus, he took his leave and went to the hermitage to enter the religious life.

By the power of the roots of goodness from his past lives, he spontaneously awakened to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without a teacher and realized the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha. He then thought:
"Previously, I made a pact with my sister; I should go to see her now."

He then went to that place, ascended into the void, and manifested spiritual transformations; fire issued from his upper body while clear water flowed from his lower body. His wondrous manifestations were manifold as he descended through the air.
When all the ordinary worldlings saw the supernormal power, their minds turned back with great speed, like a great tree collapsing to the ground; they prostrated at his venerable feet and said:
"O elder brother!"
"Now I have attained such extraordinary, sublime, and supreme virtues. He replied,
"I have realized them."
He said, "Brother,
you require food and drink for the sustenance of your body;
I seek merit and wish to offer you hospitality, so please stay here."
She replied, "You have no autonomy; you should go and inform your husband.
She then said to her husband:
"Do you not know now, O Benevolent One?
My elder brother has left the household life and perfected the prohibitive precepts, attaining the most sublime fruit, foremost in the world.
I wish to make offerings to him, yet I dare not act on my own authority."
"If you grant permission, I shall provide you with food and drink for three months. He replied, "O noble one!"
"If he had not gone forth as a monk, although I would have been unwilling, I would ultimately have had to provide for him;
how much more so now that he has already gone forth and attained the supreme Way?
Now, according to your wish, I shall provide offerings for three months."
During those three months, he provided his elder brother with all manner of excellent and superior offerings.
When the three months were complete, he immediately presented him with fine cotton cloth, a knife, and needles, offering them as gifts.
Once her elder brother had accepted it, he began to cut with the knife; the blade was exceptionally sharp and his cutting was swift.
Seeing this, his younger sister immediately squatted down and spoke these words:
"May my faculties be as sharp and swift as this knife, so that until the future, I may achieve keen wisdom."
Then the Pratyekabuddha took up the cloth and began to sew; he was skilled with needle and thread, sewing without hindrance.
The sister then made this vow:
"May my wisdom, from this life until the future, be like this needle—profound and far-reaching, penetrating all things without obstruction."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor doubts. Was the Brahmin woman of the past anyone else? [It was none other than her.]”
This is Śāriputra. Because in the past he made offerings to a pratyekabuddha, presenting him with a knife, white cotton cloth, and so forth, and extensively made aspirational prayers,
by virtue of these roots of merit, he now possesses sharp wisdom and is foremost in intelligence.
"O bhikṣus! You should know that black karma results in black retribution.
If one performs white karma, one will receive white retribution; this should be understood in detail as explained above."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed the Blessed One,
saying: "Venerable Śāriputra, what karma did he perform in the past,
such that he is now born neither into a noble lineage nor into one of extreme lowliness, but in the middle class, and has repeatedly gone forth from the household life?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Listen, all of you!
In the distant past, there was a king who, shortly after taking a wife, indulged himself in sensual pleasures and went out on hunting expeditions; before many years had passed, he fathered a son."
When his son had grown up, he saw that his father, the king, was governing the world through unrighteous means, and he thought to himself:
"Upon my father's passing, he shall surely fall into hell."
"When I succeed to the royal throne, I too shall suffer this same misery.
I ought to go forth into the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, leave the household life to practice the path, and cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to his father's presence and said:
"Great King! I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to leave the household life.
The king said to his son:
"All those who perform various sacrifices to the gods and other deities seek wealth and nobility.
You are a crown prince of the elephant-riding lineage; the royal throne is yours for the taking."
"Why do you now seek to leave the household life?
Thus he rebuked him in various ways and would not allow him to go forth.
Later, on another occasion, the Prince mounted an elephant and went out of the city for an excursion. There he saw a poor man holding leaves and begging for food, and said to him:
“O Worthy One! I am of noble lineage and cannot leave the household life.
You are not of noble lineage; why do you not leave the household life?”
He replied, "I have no robes or alms bowl; how can I go forth?
[The Buddha] answered:
“O Worthy One! I shall provide you with the three robes, the alms bowl, and other requisites; you should go forth into the homeless life. He replied:
"Excellent! At that time, the Prince bestowed [the gift] as previously instructed.
At that moment, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) who was sitting in joyful tranquility beneath a tree.
At that time, the prince and the mendicant went together to the place where the seer dwelt.
The prince dismounted from his elephant and, having approached the seer, addressed him, saying: "O Noble One!"
"I wish to go forth [into the religious life].
At that time, the seer immediately allowed him to go forth.
The prince said:
"I am now about to depart; if you should attain the Way or realize its fruits, I pray that you will inform me.
He replied, "As you have said, sir."

Having gone forth, he immediately went to a quiet place to sit in meditation and cultivate concentration. Thereupon, he spontaneously realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without a teacher and attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha. He then thought:
"The fruit I have realized is entirely due to the Prince."
"I should now go to see him and manifest miraculous transformations.

Having formed this thought, he went to that place, ascended into the air, and displayed various miracles, including emitting fire from his upper body and water from his lower body, as described at length above.

At that time, when the people had witnessed these miraculous transformations, their minds were swiftly turned around like a great tree collapsing to the ground; they all prostrated themselves and said:
"Noble One!..."
"Have you now realized such a sublime fruit?
He replied, "I have realized it."
Having seen this, the Prince thought to himself:
"All that they have obtained is entirely due to me. Were I not to leave the household life and realize this fruit, would there not be none who are born into high-ranking families?"
Having formed this thought, he made this vow:

"May we, in birth after birth and life after life, not be born into high-ranking families nor into those of low status, but be born into the middle class, so that I may be free from obstacles and easily attain renunciation."
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. As for that prince of the past, was he anyone else?
He is none other than Śāriputra.
By the power of his vows made in former times, he has now been born into the life of a renunciant, possessing mastery and being unimpeded."
One should know that the retribution for karma is experienced by oneself;

if one performs white (wholesome) karma, one receives white retribution in return, and if one performs black (unwholesome) karma, one receives black retribution in return. This applies to all good and evil deeds, as explained in detail previously.
“O bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; since only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can sever such doubts, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“By what meritorious deeds did this Venerable Śāriputra bring his roots of goodness to maturity, such that he is foremost in wisdom among the śrāvakas?
The Buddha said,
“It is due to the power of a vow he made in the distant past.”
The bhikṣus addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what vow did you make?"
"Only through the Buddha's compassion may you explain this extensively for my sake.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should listen!"
In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Śāriputra had a teacher who had gone forth under Kāśyapa Buddha. That teacher of Śāriputra was prophesied by Kāśyapa Buddha:
"Among the assembly of śrāvakas, you shall be foremost in intelligence and wisdom, and your holy life shall remain without flaw or deficiency."
"However, there is no karmic fruition; it is not that a fruit has been obtained.
When the teacher reached the end of his life, he made extensive vows:

"By the merit of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) I have practiced and by these roots of virtue, may I—along with that Brahmin Uttara—at a future time when the human lifespan is one hundred years, when a Buddha appears in the world named Śākyamuni, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the ten titles, go forth as a renunciant within his teaching, sever all afflictions, reach the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and realize the fruit of Arhatship."
"At that time, Śāriputra, the fruit he has now attained is exactly as his teacher’s wish.
By the power of that vow, Śāriputra is now foremost in wisdom among all the śrāvakas."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; since only the Buddha could resolve it, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did that venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana perform in the past?"
"His roots of goodness have matured; among all the śrāvakas, he is foremost in supernormal powers.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "You should listen!"

In the distant past, that Mahāmaudgalyāyana practiced wholesome conduct and performed wholesome deeds, accumulating roots of merit; even unto their fruition, it is explained at length as previously described.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a rishi who practiced compassion in his heart and felt pity for all sentient beings."
At that time, there was a poor woodcutter who, carrying a load of firewood, arrived at that place and lay down to rest, utterly exhausted.
Upon seeing him, the rishi felt profound compassion and thought to himself:

"This impoverished man did not plant the roots of goodness through practice in previous lives; though he has obtained a human body, he must endure such toil and hardship merely to obtain food and clothing."
"I should now deliver this person by ordaining him and causing him to practice the holy life.
Having formed this thought, he said: "Worthy son!"
"You have endured such hardship; why do you not go forth into the homeless life?
He replied, "Great Seer!"
"I am a poor man who makes his living by gathering firewood; who can see me and grant me the going forth?
He replied, "O noble one!"
"I shall deliver you and enable you to leave the household life.
Should you attain the fruit [of the path], I pray that you will repay me. He replied:
"Noble One! If you shall indeed realize the fruit of the path, you must certainly repay me.
At that time, the rishi immediately granted him ordination.

Having gone forth, he sought a quiet place to cultivate meditation and practice concentration; thereupon, he spontaneously realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without a teacher and attained the fruit of a pratyekabuddha. He then thought:
"The fruit I have realized is entirely due to the rishi."
"I ought to fulfill my vow by going to see him and report back.

Having formed this thought, he went to the place where the seer was, ascended into the void, and manifested the eighteen transformations, such as causing clear water to flow downward and even emitting fire, as described at length previously.
Upon seeing this, the seer’s mind turned swiftly like a great tree collapsing to the ground; he then made this vow:
"May the immeasurable merit I have cultivated result in me possessing, in a future life, the same majesty as yours and becoming foremost in supernormal powers."
"O bhikṣus! Do not harbor any other thoughts.
As for that rishi of the past, could he have been anyone else?"
This was none other than Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
You should know that the retributions of black and white karma, etc., are as explained at length above. You bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; since only the Buddha could resolve them, they came to the Buddha and said:
"By what karma did this Mahāmaudgalyāyana become foremost in supernormal powers among the Venerable Ones?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “You should listen!
Long ago, in the past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, it was due to his vow, as described in detail above.”
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; since only the Buddha could resolve them, they came to the World-Honored One and said:
"What wholesome karma did the Venerable Kauṇḍinya perform in a previous life?"
"His roots of goodness have matured; he possesses the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) and now has sharp faculties and clear understanding.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In this present Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in the past named Kāśyapa. There was a teacher who practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) but did not attain its fruit. At the time of his death, because he made a vow—as previously explained in detail—[he attained this result]."
During the time when the Buddha was dwelling in the world, whenever there were those who had gone forth and received full ordination, they would all come to the presence of the World-Honored One;
the Buddha would then say: "Welcome, bhikṣu!"

His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the kāṣāya robe was donned upon his body, and he naturally held an almsbowl; he was thus immediately ordained as a bhikṣu and received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
Separately, there was another man in a distant foreign land who came to the place of the bhikṣus seeking to go forth.
That bhikṣu took this person to the presence of the Buddha, intending to grant him the going forth and full ordination.
However, the man died on the way and thus was unable to receive the going forth.
At that time, the bhikṣus, on account of this matter, came to inform the Buddha, reporting everything as previously described.
Then the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"My śrāvakas are weary. If there is anyone who seeks to go forth and receive full ordination (upasampadā) while residing in a distant land, I permit them to receive the going forth and full ordination within the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, the Blessed One gathered the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"Because of this matter, from this day forward, if there are those who seek to go forth, I permit the community of bhikṣus to grant them the going forth and the full ordination."
After the Buddha had granted permission for this matter, the community of bhikṣus did not know how to grant them the going forth or the full ordination (upasampadā).
They reported this situation to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"However, when anyone comes seeking to leave the household life, one should inquire about various obstacles.
If there are no hindrances, only then should one confer the Three Refuges.

One should then have them join their palms and kneel on their right knees, and they should personally declare their name, saying: 'For as long as this life lasts, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Most Honored among Two-legged Beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the Most Honored in Freedom from Desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the Most Honored among the Assembly.'"
"Subsequently, he was granted the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the two hundred and fifty precepts,
as explained in detail elsewhere.
Once he had completed his renunciation and full ordination (*upasampadā*), he felt no fear or hesitation toward his *ācārya* and *upādhyāya*, and did not inquire about anything he was required to do.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a training rule for my disciples: [text continues]"

If a disciple performs tasks such as sprinkling water on the ground, smearing the altar with *gomaya*, sweeping the floor, mending robes and bowls, or eating and drinking, they must inform their teacher. Furthermore, if a guest bhikṣu who was previously unknown arrives in one's room, one should inform the teacher so that he may know.
With the exception of five matters, all others must be announced.
If one does not act accordingly, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

The five matters are: chewing a tooth-stick, drinking pure water, performing the great or small excretions, and prostrating before a caitya within a distance of forty-nine fathoms; these do not require announcement to the two teachers.
Regarding all matters such as sewing clothes and the like, the disciple should say:
"Teacher, do not trouble yourself; I shall perform these tasks on your behalf.
If they act in this manner, it is well.
If one does not act in this manner, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
If the preceptor performs meritorious deeds or acts on behalf of the assembly, there is no offense if one does not assist.
If either of the two preceptors is ill, one must diligently attend to them and should address the preceptor as follows:
Regarding the medical requisites, food, and drink required, one should comply with the teacher's wishes and must not act contrary to their intent.
If one acts in this manner, it is well;
if one does not, one incurs an offense as previously described.
If either of the two teachers commits an offense, a co-resident disciple should skillfully employ means to say to them:
"Teacher, you have committed such an offense of *duṣkṛta*; you should confess it."
The details are as explained above.
Since the two masters held wrong views, the great assembly expelled them from their residence through acts such as formal censure.
The disciples must then earnestly seek forgiveness from the assembly, causing the community to rejoice.
Furthermore, one must inform the teacher, saying: "Do not harbor evil views.
One should skillfully and correctly admonish him to abandon this matter, so that the community and the teacher may dwell in harmony and happiness.

If one does not act thus, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma; this should be understood in detail as explained above. If the two masters commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, the disciple must cause the masters to confess it.
Furthermore, if the Saṃgha grants those two teachers the parivāsa penance and the mānāpya probation, they must not share a room for sleeping or engage in similar activities with virtuous bhikṣus.

If one repents according to the Dharma, the roots of transgression and the karma shall all be completely extinguished; one will become equal to a virtuous bhikṣu, and so forth, until the restoration of one's original status, as explained in detail above.
If one acts in this manner, it is well;
if one does not comply with this practice, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
His disciples should earnestly admonish him and urge him toward repentance.
"If a disciple commits a transgression, the teacher must also earnestly reprimand them and cause them to reform.
