Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the venerable Upasena, while traveling through the countryside, completed his three-month rains retreat and ordained a disciple; he then proceeded gradually with him toward the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Upasena, having washed his feet, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they first say: "Welcome!"
"From where have you come?
And in which direction did you observe the three-month rains retreat?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Upāli:
“From which direction have you come?
Where did you observe the three-month rains retreat?
The bhikṣu Upacāra replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have come from another country; there, I sat for the three-month rains retreat.
The Buddha asked:
“Whose disciple is this good man? Upatiṣya replied, “He is my disciple.”
The Buddha asked,
"How long has it been since you went forth? He replied:
"Two years have passed since he [Upasena] ordained, yet his disciple has been ordained for only one year.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"This Upasena has already committed an offense by acting as a preceptor for one who has not yet completed a full year of ordination. I now establish this rule for all bhikṣus: you must not ordain another disciple or confer the full precepts (upasampadā) upon them if you have not yourself been ordained for a full year. Furthermore, you should not live together with such a person; rather, you should rely upon others for your dependence (niśraya)."
If one has left the household life but has not yet completed ten years of seniority, one should not ordain a śrāmaṇera nor confer full ordination (upasampadā) upon them.
If a guest monk arrives whom one does not previously know, one should not grant him formal reliance (niśraya).

If one has completed ten years of seniority and is well-versed in the points of obstruction and non-obstruction within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, one should ordain śrāmaṇeras and perform all duties such as providing formal reliance (niśraya).
It is impossible for one who has not yet disciplined oneself to discipline others.

Likewise, it is improper to attempt to deliver those who are foolish and immature; it is likewise impossible for one who has not personally realized liberation, tranquility, and nirvana to explain them to others.
"Having fallen oneself into the mire and not yet emerged from it, to intend to deliver others is likewise unreasonable.
At that time, there was an elderly, ignorant bhikṣu who was unacquainted with the Vinaya; he ordained an outsider and conferred full ordination upon him.
Having received full ordination, he said to his upādhyāya, "Now, please instruct me.
The teacher did not understand and remained silent without responding; consequently, the student gave rise to feelings of derision and resentment.
The bhikṣus, having understood this, informed the Buddha of the circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"I now permit bhikṣus with ten years of seniority to ordain disciples. Their full ordination shall be as previously described, and they shall not remain in dependence upon others."
And one accomplishes five qualities. What are these five?
First, having been fully ordained for more than ten years;
Second, when a disciple is ill, one is able to provide care and nursing;
third, when there are instances of misconduct or doubts regarding transgressions, one admonishes them according to the specific matter;
fourth, if there are wrong views, one instructs them so as to bring about right view.
Fifth, if they do not delight in the Dharma, one should diligently gather them in so that they may dwell in delight.
These are called the five dharmas.
Furthermore, there are another five kinds.
What are these five?
First, being endowed with ethical discipline; second, being learned; third, upholding the Sūtras; fourth, upholding the Vinaya; and fifth, skillfully upholding the Mātṛkā—these are called the five.
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are these five?

First, being endowed with precepts without deficiency; second, being widely learned; third, being well-versed in the meaning of the sūtras; fourth, being well-acquainted with the points of penetration and obstruction within the Vinaya; and fifth, being well-versed in the principles and purports of the Mātṛkā-piṭaka. These are called the five.
Furthermore, there are five kinds.

What are these five? First, possessing the precepts; second, being learned; third, upholding the sūtras and knowing their meaning; fourth, being well-versed in the Vinaya; and fifth, being well-clarified in the Mātṛkā-piṭaka. These are called the five, as explained in detail previously.
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are these five?
These five are the same as the preceding ones; however, for each one, the word "extreme" (*atīva*) is added, as explained in detail above.
Furthermore, there are five kinds; these five are also the same, with the character "superior" (śeṣa) added above each one.
Again, there are five kinds, explained in the same manner as above, with the character "capable" (śakya) added above, as explained at length previously.
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are the five?

First, accomplishment in ethical discipline; second, accomplishment in extensive learning; third, accomplishment in superior liberation; fourth, accomplishment in the superior liberation of realized knowledge; and fifth, accomplishment in wisdom. These are called the five.

Furthermore, there are five kinds: first, accomplishment in faith; second, accomplishment in ethical discipline; third, accomplishment in extensive learning; fourth, accomplishment in relinquishment; and fifth, accomplishment in wisdom. These are explained in detail as previously stated.
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are the five?

First, possession of ethical discipline; second, extensive learning; third, diligence; fourth, mindfulness; and fifth, wisdom. These are called the five; the detailed explanation is the same as before.
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are these five?
First, the possession of ethical discipline; second, extensive learning; third, diligence; fourth, meditative concentration; and fifth, wisdom.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are another five kinds: four are as above, and the fifth is this—delighting in sitting in quietude.
Again, there are five kinds:

First, the accomplishment of the aggregate of ethical discipline of one in training; second, the accomplishment of the aggregate of meditative concentration of one in training; third, the accomplishment of the aggregate of wisdom of one in training; fourth, the accomplishment of the aggregate of liberation of one in training; fifth, the accomplishment of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one in training—as explained at length elsewhere.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of accomplishment for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which are explained in the same manner as for those in training (*śaikṣa*).
There are another five kinds:
first, knowing of transgression; second, indication; third, mental indication; fourth, relinquishment; and fifth, understanding according to [the teaching].
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are these five?

First, knowing when there are obstacles; second, knowing when there are no obstacles; third, providing instruction according to what has been taught; fourth, granting formal reliance (*niśraya*) to a disciple; and fifth, receiving [them into the community]. These are explained in detail as previously stated.
Furthermore, there are five kinds. What are the five?

First, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense; third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy; and fifth, knowing how to provide a detailed explanation and exposition of the Prātimokṣa.

One who has accomplished five qualities and completed ten years of seniority may ordain others through the full admission (*upasampadā*), provide them with dependence (*niśraya*), and give them instruction; however, if one does not personally possess these aforementioned five qualities, one must rely upon another for dependence.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"If one has already accomplished the five dharmas and completed ten years since full ordination, one should ordain disciples, and one should not oneself rely upon another for dependence.
If a bhikṣu has been fully ordained for sixty years but does not understand the Prātimokṣa, and does not accomplish the five dharmas, should he rely upon another for his residence?
The Buddha said,
"You should dwell in dependence upon another. He replied:
“What is the basis for this?
The Buddha said,
“It is based on the elder.”
He said, "If there is no elder, how should one abide?
The Buddha said:
"One should rely upon those who are junior, except for prostrating; in all other matters, one should accept their instructions.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

There was a bhikṣu who was foolish and lacked wisdom, being unacquainted with what is wholesome and what is unwholesome; he subsequently ordained a non-Buddhist and conferred full ordination upon him.

This individual then constantly engaged in contentious debate with the other bhikṣus, whereupon he returned to lay life, spreading various slanders and insults, which gave rise to public censure and disdain.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"How could such a thing be?
Foolish and lacking wisdom, they abandon the sublime Dharma and Vinaya to follow false views."
For example, it is like a person driven by the fire of hunger who abandons fine food and eats various foul and impure things.
Such a person is just like this: due to that ignorance, they abandon the excellent Dharma and Vinaya, taking pleasure instead in the false views of external paths.
Therefore, bhikṣus should not arbitrarily ordain non-Buddhists as disciples; they should ordain only Śākyas.

If there is a Śākya who comes wearing the robes of a non-Buddhist seeking to go forth and receive full ordination (upasampadā), such a person should be ordained so as to establish the nature of a bhikṣu.
"Except for those of the Śākya clan, all other followers of external paths should undergo a four-month period of communal residence.

Having already granted permission for the ordination of followers of external paths, [the Buddha] prescribed that they must reside together for four months, serving and making offerings while not discarding their original robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know the rules for communal residence or the procedures for ordination. They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"If any non-Buddhist comes seeking to leave the household life, you should first ask whether they are free from physical impediments."
If there are no obstacles or hindrances, bestow upon them the three refuges and the five precepts.
Then, leading them before the assembly in the presence of the Saṃgha, have them crouch with palms joined and instruct them to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"I am a follower of an external path, named [Name], and now I seek to go forth.
During the four months of the rainy season, I shall provide for the Saṃgha with my own robes; I pray that the assembly will grant me permission."
Once he has been placed where he can be seen by the eyes but cannot be heard by the ears, one bhikṣu should be appointed to perform the *karmavācanā*, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

This non-Buddhist practitioner [name], now seeks to go forth from the household life; he shall, for a period of four months, wear his original robes and provide offerings to the upādhyāya and the Saṃgha.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission;
if not, let those who object speak.
Thus he speaks three times.
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold it.
For four months, he shall perform all duties together with a śrāmaṇera, wear the robes of his preceptor, and eat the food of the Saṃgha.
"During these four months, if those with old views change them, they should be granted ordination;
if their hearts delight in non-Buddhist paths, they should be driven out.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
“As the Buddha has said:
‘Revising former views. How is it to be known that one revises former views?
The Buddha said:
"One should, before that person, praise the Three Jewels and speak of the Buddha’s virtues; one should disparage the non-Buddhists and criticize them in various ways.
If, upon hearing praise of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or hearing disparagement of their own original clan, they feel joy in their heart, one should grant them ordination."

If one’s mind is not pleased when the Three Jewels are praised, and if one feels sorrow and distress upon hearing the disparagement of non-Buddhists, then one should not be ordained; rather, one should be expelled.
However, if upon hearing the disparagement of the various non-Buddhist sects, one feels no resentment but instead gives rise to joy, this indicates that one has changed one's former views.
The Buddha said:
"If there are fire-worshipping non-Buddhists who come seeking to go forth, you should grant them ordination and bestow upon them full admission (upasampadā). Why is this? Because..."
This matter belongs to the category of fire; it is based on faith in three kinds of karma.
What are these three? They are:
existing karma, karma that has been performed, and karma that serves as the cause for performance. Therefore, one should cross over [this fire].
"O bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way:
'We shall study these karmas, as well as the karma that consists of what has been done and the karma that is the cause of what has been done.'"
The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground near Rājagṛha, having completed his three-month rains retreat.
At that time, the number of senior bhikṣus in Rājagṛha was small, while those who were junior were numerous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to go to the Southern Mountains to travel among the people, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should inform the bhikṣus:
'Those who wish to follow the World-Honored One should prepare their robes (cīvara).'"
Then Ānanda, having received this instruction, went to various places and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The World-Honored One intends to travel through the human realm; those who wish to follow the World-Honored One should prepare their robes (cīvara)."
Then the senior bhikṣu said to the venerable Ānanda,
"I cannot travel with the Blessed One. Ānanda replied:
"Why cannot we? They replied, "We are old."
Then the youths said, "We will not go. He asked:
"Why? He replied, "Since my preceptor will not go with me, I must now attend upon my upādhyāya."

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by a few disciples and fully equipped with robes and bowls, set out for the human realm and traveled along the road. He looked left and right like a great elephant king, fearing that the bhikṣus might hold their water jars and bowls in an improper manner.
The World-Honored One looked back and saw that the number of bhikṣus was not large.
Knowing the reason, he asked Ānanda intentionally, saying:
"For what reason has the assembly of bhikṣus diminished?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“I now authorize those bhikṣus who have passed five summer retreats and who have accomplished five qualities to train wherever they please, to travel through the human world, and not to remain in formal dependence upon others.”

What are these five dharmas? First, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what constitutes no offense; third, knowing grave offenses; fourth, knowing minor offenses; and fifth, skillfully upholding the *Bhikṣu-Prātimokṣa* and being able to expound it extensively. These are called the five dharmas by which one may travel among people and receive instruction wherever one goes; you may proceed without doubt.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If more than six years have passed and one has accomplished the five dharmas, is it permissible to travel among the people to receive instruction?”
The Buddha said, “He has.
He then addressed the World-Honored One again:
"Having completed three summer retreats and accomplished five dharmas, may one go [to the assembly] or not?
The Buddha said, "One may not."
The Buddha said:
"I shall now establish a regulation: those who have completed five summer retreats and have accomplished five dharmas may go as they please.
If one has not yet fulfilled these requirements, even if they are well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, they should not travel abroad to study."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen youths as renunciants and conferred full ordination upon them.
All of these were young children, with Upāli at their head; they had endured hunger throughout the night and were weeping until dawn.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked and said to Ānanda:
"For what reason are there the sounds of crying children in the middle of the night?"
Ānanda reported the circumstances in full, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a regulation:
if one has not reached twenty years of age, one must not be granted full ordination (upasampadā) to attain the status of a bhikṣu."
Why is this? Those who have not yet reached twenty years of age cannot endure hunger, cold, heat, thirst, exhaustion, the bites of mosquitoes and insects, illness, and the like.
Furthermore, they are unable to endure the reprimands of their teachers, as well as various forms of suffering and distress.
"Because they are young and small, they cannot endure the aforementioned sufferings such as these.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If they have reached twenty years of age, they will possess resolute vigor and be able to endure the aforementioned sufferings of rebukes and the like."
Because there are such faults in conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon one whose age is not yet complete,
for this reason, monks, if one has not reached twenty years of age, you should not confer full ordination upon them.
If there is a śrāmaṇera who comes seeking full ordination (upasampadā),
the bhikṣu should ask:
"Are you twenty years of age?"
"If one does not inquire [about this], one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a householder in this city who, shortly after marrying his wife, fathered a son; as the child grew, he gradually reached maturity.
As the householder’s family estate gradually dissipated, he thought to himself:
"I am now impoverished; I ought to seek ordination.
He then addressed his son, saying:
"I am now old and cannot carry on the family business with you.
I now wish to go forth in that well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; what do you think?"
The son said to his father, "If you,
father, go forth from the household life, I too should now follow you and go forth.
The father replied:
"Very well.
Thereupon, the father and son went together to the Jetavana Grove and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Noble ones!..."
"I wish to go forth as a renunciant together with you.
The bhikṣu replied, "Very well."
He spoke again, saying:
"O worthy one! To what relative of yours does this young boy belong?"
He replied, "This son also wishes to leave the household life.
Then those bhikṣus together ordained him, instructing him in the four dignified postures as well as in eating.
After several days had passed, he said to him:
"Go; deer do not raise deer. The city of Śrāvastī is my domain;
it is exceedingly vast, populous, and its inhabitants have deep faith and devotion toward the Triple Gem."
"You should go there and seek food and clothing for yourself to sustain your life.
Having heard these words, he took up his robes and bowl and, accompanied by [the others], went to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in due order.
Thereupon, on a public road, he saw a woman making fried cakes.
At that time, the novice monk immediately begged from her, and the woman replied,
"Give me the price."
The śrāmaṇera replied, "I am a śramaṇa; I do not possess wealth or goods.
Since he did not pay the price, he failed to obtain the cakes.
At that time, the novice cried out loudly, rolling about on the ground.
Thereupon, the people there began to mock and criticize him, saying:
"Why has this bhikṣu ordained this mass of blood?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"All these faults arise from ordaining those who are too young.
From this day forward, one shall not grant ordination to anyone who has not reached fifteen years of age."
If a youth comes seeking to go forth, the bhikṣu should ask:
"Are you fifteen years of age?
If he does not ask this, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Upānanda had two novices who amused themselves with one another, like a woman playing with a man, or as a man plays with a woman.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"All these faults arise from keeping two śrāmaṇeras.
If one keeps them, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
After the Buddha had established this rule, there were two brothers of nearly the same age who came seeking ordination.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to ordain them and did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are brothers who simultaneously seek to go forth, they should be ordained; there is no offense.
Since those two novices have not yet reached the required age, one should remain behind to instruct the other in his duties."
One should entrust him to a close friend or to a person of great virtue.
When he reaches the required age, one should grant him full ordination (*upasampadā*).
As for those who have not yet reached that age, there is no offense in supporting them oneself.

"If one is twenty years of age and does not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) together with them, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma. This was said by the Buddha while he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was a householder who had a servant; the servant was diligent in his labors without any laziness, completing all tasks before anyone else.
Later, at another time, the master became angry and thought to himself:
"This master is very difficult to serve; I should run away.
He then thought again:
"It is difficult to abandon one's place of birth; these śrāvaka sons of the Śākyas have received favor from the king, and none can harm them. I shall go to that place and leave the household life."
The slave immediately went to the Jeta Grove and said to the bhikṣus:
"Noble ones! I wish to seek ordination."

Then the bhikṣus immediately granted him the going-forth and the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having been instructed in various ways, he practiced and investigated according to those teachings; he was able to eliminate all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship, as described at length elsewhere.
At that time, the elder gave rise to a sense of regret and thought to himself:
"In all the work my slave performed, there was not a single instance of laziness.
I ought not to have been angry and caused him to abandon me."
"If I were to see him, I should ask for his forgiveness.
He then stood by the city gate in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for food.
He saw him and addressed him, saying:
"O worthy one! Have you been able to go forth into the homeless life?"
He replied, "Yes. The other said:
"Now there is no one to serve me; let us return home together.
At that time, the bhikṣu ascended into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations.
At that time, the householder felt remorse and quickly returned to faith; his mind turned back as swiftly as a great tree being toppled over. Prostrating at his feet, he said:
"Noble One!..."
"Having attained such spiritual power as this, I pray that from this day forward you will accept my robes, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal requisites.
His fame spread everywhere:
"The slave so-and-so has gone forth and realized the fruit of Arhatship, possessing such supreme and wondrous merits."
When King Prasenajit heard these words, he said:
"A certain elder has a slave who has gone forth as a monk; he has attained a most excellent realization and is able to obtain the four fruits."
Having spoken these words, he immediately summoned his ministers and addressed them, saying:

"You should know that I am of the consecrated Kṣatriya royal lineage. From this day forward, if there are slaves in the households of any officials, elders, or others who seek to leave the household life, you must allow them to go forth and not create any obstacles."

In the city of Śrāvastī, there was at that time an elder who had a slave. He was diligent in his labors and never grew weary; as described in detail previously, he then went forth into homelessness and received full ordination. Having been instructed in the monastic rules, the Master addressed him, saying: "O worthy one!"
Deer do not raise deer; Śrāvastī is a vast land where your parents reside.
You should now go there to beg for food and sustain yourself.
At that time, the householder felt regret in his heart and thought to himself:
"That slave was diligent in his tasks and never grew weary; when I see him, I should ask for his forgiveness."
At that time, the householder stood beside the gate of Śrāvastī.
Then, at the hour of eating, the bhikṣu put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Having seen this, the elder said to him:
"Noble sir! Now that you have gone forth, who will attend to me?"
"Let us return home together.
He then took hold of the bhikṣu’s arm, whereupon the bhikṣu said,
"If you touch me, I shall cut off your wrist."
"King Prasenajit has issued an edict bestowing his favor upon the bhikṣus, treating them as if they were crown princes.
The elder then reviled the bhikṣu, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have ruined my city walls and destroyed the brahmins; how could it be appropriate to allow a slave to go forth into the religious life?"
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Since such a fault exists, from now on, you bhikṣus must not grant ordination to slaves."
If there is one who seeks ordination, you should ask them:
"Are you a slave? If one grants ordination to a slave, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was a householder who, whenever he issued a loan, would sometimes collect only the interest, and sometimes collect both the principal and the interest.

Later, at another time, he saw the debtor again; when both principal and interest were demanded, the creditor dragged him away, held him for a long time, and would not release him, until they finally established a deadline before he was let go to return home.
That man then thought to himself:
"This householder is indeed of a very wicked disposition, and I am unable to return both the principal and the interest; I shall flee."
Again, he thought to himself:
"One's native land is difficult to abandon; yet these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are like crown princes even in the presence of the king. Should I now seek to go forth from home under them?"
He immediately went to the Jetavana Grove, approached the bhikṣus, and said:
"Noble ones! I seek to go forth."
He granted him the going forth and the full ordination, and instructed him in the disciplinary rules.
Having attained full ordination, he applied himself with courageous diligence; without interruption and before long, he realized the fruit of arhatship.
Then that householder felt regret and thought to himself:
"He owes me a debt and has always returned both principal and interest from time to time; for what reason have I suddenly cast him aside with such contempt?"
"If I should see him again at this time, I shall offer my apologies.
He then stood waiting at the city gate.
At the first part of the day, that bhikṣu took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms.
The elder saw him and asked, "Worthy sir!
Although you have already gone forth, you still occasionally return to retrieve your principal and interest; you may come home with me now."
He then took him by the hand, intending to lead him away.
At that moment, the bhikṣu immediately ascended into the air and manifested various eighteen kinds of supernatural transformations, as described in detail above.
At that time, the householder quickly developed faith; his mind turned back with such speed as a great tree collapsing to the ground.
He said, "Noble One!..."

Having attained such sublime virtues and the realization of this supreme fruit, from this day forward, I shall provide the noble one with all necessary requisites, clothing, and food; I pray that you will graciously accept them.
At that time, throughout the four quarters, everyone heard and knew that the creditor to whom the householder so-and-so owed money had received such a fruit [of his debt].
When King Jayasena heard of this matter, he commanded his ministers, saying:
"From this day forward, regarding all debts that have not yet been repaid, if those who owe them wish to go forth in the presence of the Buddha, you must not create any obstacles for them."
At that time, there was a householder in the city of Śrāvastī who lent money at interest.
There was a man who borrowed goods to generate profit, and so forth, until he eventually went forth into homelessness; he did not keep deer and so on, as described in detail above.
On another occasion, while he was walking for alms with his bowl, the elder encountered him and said,
"Bhikṣu! Since you have already gone forth, who will now pay me back my principal and interest from time to time?"
"Now we may return together.
As he wished to take his hand, the bhikṣu said, "Do not touch me!"
"If you touch me, I shall cut off your hand. He replied, "Why?"
The bhikṣu said: "Have you not heard the royal decree?
For those who wish to renounce the world, all debts shall be fully remitted."
They criticized him together, saying these words:
"The renunciant sons of the Śākyas harbor much arrogance; they take those currently burdened by debt and ordain them as monks."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Because of ordaining those who are in debt, such faults have arisen.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, those who owe debts should not be ordained indiscriminately.
Should anyone ordain them, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, begot a son;
as the boy gradually grew up, he fled in secret because his father had rebuked him with anger.
Later, he had this thought:
"It is difficult to leave one's native land; however, all the Śākyas are like princes and are exempt from various duties.
It would be appropriate for me now to go forth as a renunciant there."
He immediately went to the Jeta Grove, approached the bhikṣus,
and said, "Noble ones!
I wish to go forth."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who immediately granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Later, at another time, his father sought out his son, went to the bhikṣu’s place, and said:
"Noble One!..."
"Did you see such a youth coming?
He replied, "He has already been ordained."
The householder said,
"Do these bhikṣus always carry knives?
To everyone who comes, they immediately shave their hair."
He asked again, "Did you not wait for seven or eight days? For what reason did you ordain him immediately?
The bhikṣu reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not ordain them immediately.
If there is a youth who comes from not far from home seeking to leave the household life and become a monk, one should wait for seven or eight days before ordaining him."
"If there is someone coming from afar who wishes to go forth, there is no offense in granting him ordination within seven or eight days.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son. At that time, the householder said to his wife, "O fair-faced one!
Although raising my son causes me some loss, I now wish to go to a foreign land to engage in trade."
"The debt I owe, let my son repay it.
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed and did not return.
His wife raised him, and as the boy gradually grew up, she sent him to a school to study the non-Buddhist scriptures.
Among his fellow students, all were thoroughly proficient in the various treatises, yet this boy alone had gained nothing at all.
On another occasion, his mother went to the school and said to the teacher, "We pay the same tuition as everyone else;
why is it that while all the others are fully equipped in their studies, my child understands nothing?"
The doctor replied:
"Regarding that which is studied, there are two kinds of matters through which one's studies achieve completion. What are these two?
"First, one possesses a sense of shame; second, one has fear.
Yet this boy lacks both of these entirely.
His mother replied:
"Why does the teacher not give me a staff?
On another occasion, as soon as the teacher struck him, he was rebuked in various ways and immediately began to weep;
returning to his mother, he related the matter in detail, whereupon his mother struck him as well.
Then the boy thought to himself: "I have met with misfortune;
previously I was beaten in one place, and now I have encountered it in two. I cannot endure this suffering; I should flee and enter the Jeta Grove."
Upon arriving there, he saw a śrāmaṇera gathering flowers and immediately exclaimed,
"How very joyful! He then asked:
"Why? He replied, "To leave the household life."
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"Why do you not go forth into homelessness now? He answered:
“Noble One! Who can grant me the going forth? He replied:
"Come! Let us go together to question the upādhyāya.
Having seen the teacher, he addressed him, saying:
“Upādhyāya! This son of good family wishes to seek renunciation.
Thereupon, his preceptor immediately granted him the going forth.
Later, his mother went to the schoolhouse and asked the teacher,
"Where is my son? The teacher replied:
"I struck him and he fled back home.
His mother immediately replied, "I saw him returning and struck him again; he abandoned me and ran away."

At that time, her compassionate mother went to various places to search for and seek him out, but finding no trace of him, she stood at the gate of the city of Rājagṛha, gazing toward the east and the west.
After standing for no long time, she saw the youth, having shaved off his hair and beard, coming along with that novice, both carrying their water-pots and bowls.
When the mother recognized him, she struck her breast with her hand and wailed in grief, saying:
"O foolish son!"
"I have searched everywhere without exception, traveling through all directions, yet I could not find you;
there has been no news of you. Why have you now gone forth among these lowly śramaṇas?"
Taking him by the hand, he led him back home, stripped him of his robes and bowl, and compelled him to return to lay life.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"To grant ordination to one who has not informed his parents gives rise to many faults."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish this regulation:
if anyone ordains someone who has not informed their parents, that person commits an offense against the Dharma."
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Pond in the Bamboo Grove near Rājagṛha.
In this city, there was a brahmin who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son.
As he grew older, he suddenly fell ill; he consulted physicians everywhere, but none could cure him.
His mother said to her son, "You should seek treatment for your illness from the elder Jīvaka."
Having arrived at that place, he said:
"Householder! Please treat my illness."
The elder said, "Your illness is grave and difficult to treat; however, my medical practice treats only two kinds of people. What are these two?"
"First, there are the Buddha and the Saṃgha; second, there are the people within the royal palace.
Your illness cannot be treated at this time; you must now return home.
The son immediately returned, and his mother asked him:
"Is that illness curable? He replied,
"My illness cannot be treated by anyone."
He related everything as previously described.
His mother said to her son,
"You should go forth into the religious life."
The son replied to his mother, saying, "I am of the Brahmin caste; how can I go forth as a renunciant among these mixed-caste śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?
She then said to her son:
"You may first go forth as a monk; if your illness is cured, it will not be difficult to return to lay life.
The son said, "If I am to go forth, my head must surely be shaved. How can this be?"
The mother said, "There is no need to worry about the hair not growing back; that would be impossible.
Once it grows back later, what is there to fear?"
He immediately went to the Bamboo Grove, approached the bhikṣus, prostrated at their feet,
and said: "Noble ones,
grant me the going forth."
Having already gone forth, he stayed outside the door during that night and did not enter the room; the teacher then asked him, "Why do you not come in?"
He replied, "My body is ill; I am unable to enter.
The Master then said:
"You have now gone forth as a renunciant;
how could you possibly be ill? He replied, "Upādhyāya!"
"While I was still a layman, I previously suffered from this illness.
The Master said, "Why did you not tell me?"
He replied, "The teacher did not ask me.
His teacher then became angry.
When morning had arrived, his former disciples all came to request an audience and asked: "Upādhyāya!
Why are you not joyful?"
The Master then said:
"My dwelling is a clinic for the sick.
All those who are ill come to seek refuge here."
The śrāmaṇera said: "As the Blessed One has taught, there are two matters:
first, one should not carry heavy burdens; second, once someone has been delivered across, one should not abandon them."
"The Master has now passed away; what do you intend to do?
While these words were being spoken, Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, arrived.
The Master said to the physician, "Is this bhikṣu’s illness curable or not?"
The King of Physicians replied, "This illness is extremely grave; however, if King Prasenajit provides sufficient medicine, I shall treat it.
Once the treatment was successfully concluded, he addressed his preceptor, saying:
"I have come forth from home seeking a certain matter.
Now that my purpose has been accomplished, I wish to return.
The Master said:
"Have you attained the fruit of arhatship?
He replied, "I have not yet attained it."
He asked again:
"Have you attained the fruit of non-returning, once-returning, or stream-entry?
They all replied: [No.]
"Not yet. "For what reason have you returned? He replied:
“I have entered this monastic life because of illness; now that my illness has been cured, how can I remain here?
The Master said, “Within the Dharma of renunciation there are four supreme fruits, none of which you have yet attained.”
"You should stay here for now and repay your debt for the medicine;
if you do not, you will surely die from falling ill again in the future.
Disregarding his teacher's words, he immediately departed.
Out of gratitude for his kindness, he provided Puṣkarasārin with flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks.
At that time, Puṣkarasārin said to him: "O noble one!"
"What do you seek from me? That brahmin replied, "I seek nothing; it is merely to repay your kindness."
The householder replied,
"What further benefit have I provided for you? He answered:
"I was afflicted by illness, and through your treatment,
I have recovered. Then Jīvaka replied,
"I am not aware of having done so."
He replied, “I shall exercise mindfulness so that I may recall and understand it. Then Jīvaka said:
"You have gone forth within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; you ought to realize one of the four fruits of the śrāmaṇya.
Having accepted the offerings of others' faith, you have now instead fallen into evil deeds."
Having spoken these words, he thought to himself:
"I should go to the place where the World-Honored One is.
He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
However, because these bhikṣus allow the sick to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), it causes the King’s granaries to gradually diminish.
I too am physically exhausted, and furthermore, I am deprived of the opportunity to cultivate wholesome dharmas for the sake of the Noble Ones.”
"I pray that the World-Honored One will establish a rule so that no further sick persons are ordained.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had silently consented, Jīvaka prostrated himself and departed.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"All these faults arise entirely from my having treated those sick persons.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“From this day forward, you should not ordain those who have illnesses. If someone comes seeking to go forth, you must first ask whether they have any illness.
If you do not ask, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.”
The Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu.
At that time, King Śuddhodana issued a proclamation:
"Among the Śākyas of Kapilavastu, one son from each household shall renounce the household life."
When those kinsmen and relatives came to see him, the renunciant preached the Dharma to them.
Having heard the Dharma and rejoiced, they all gave rise to faith and immediately went forth as monastics.
Among them may be fathers, brothers, husbands, paternal uncles, or sons; they are all filled with grief and distress, weeping aloud at both the morning and evening watches of the day and night.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard the sound of those Śākyas weeping, asked:
"For what reason do these Śākyas wail with such piteous voices during both the day and night?"
Then the Śākyas addressed the king, saying:
"If our kinsmen were in the forest, those noble ones would have caused them to go forth into homelessness; it is for this reason that we are distressed and weep."
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself,
"I should go to where the Buddha is.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me one wish.
The World-Honored One asked:
“Great King! What wish do you seek?
The king replied:
"I have a small wish. However, the Śākyas say:
'The World-Honored One shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King and travel through the four continents by means of the void; we, too, shall follow the World-Honored One.'"
"Once he has gone forth, we shall not obtain at all what we had hoped for.
Furthermore, Nanda was destined to become a powerful Wheel-Turning King;
yet the World-Honored One also caused him to go forth, thereby cutting off that hope as well."

Rāhula possesses great majesty and virtue and was destined to become a great king; now that the World-Honored One has caused him to leave the household life as well, our hopes for the Śākya clan have been extinguished.
"Venerable Sir!

The affection between parents and children is most profound. We pray that the World-Honored One will establish a rule: if parents have not granted permission, do not allow their children to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the request of the King, his father.
Having received permission, the king prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
The Buddha then thought:
"All such faults arise from granting ordination and full admission to those who have not first asked their parents for permission."
"If anyone comes seeking to leave the household life, one should first ask their parents for permission before allowing them to go forth.
If one allows them to go forth without first asking, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
After the Blessed One had established the rule that one may not go forth without having asked one’s parents and received their permission,
there were those who came from distant regions whose parents had already granted them permission to go forth.
The bhikṣus did not dare to ordain them arbitrarily, and thus there was a lapse in the practice.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one has come from afar, or if their parents have previously granted permission for them to go forth, they should be allowed to go forth; there is no offense in not inquiring further."
