At that time, the merchant leaders and their company returned to the seashore; having endured hardships at sea, they were all overcome with exhaustion and fell fast asleep.
At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita beheld this great ocean and thought to himself:
"As the Buddha has said:
'There are five things which one never tires of beholding.'"

What are the five? First, the elephant king endowed with auspicious marks; second, the wheel-turning sage king; third, the great ocean; fourth, Sumeru, the king of mountains; and fifth, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"These are called the five.
Having observed for a long while, he fell asleep at the fifth watch.
At that time, the caravan leaders readied the elephant-carts and departed with their goods.
When morning arrived, they did not see Saṃgharakṣita; they were greatly alarmed and hurriedly searched in all four directions, yet in the end they could not find him.
Among them, some said:
"We should go forward."
Some said, "He was behind us. Having searched the four directions and not seeing him anywhere, they were all filled with grief and distress, saying:
"We have abandoned the Noble One; this is not auspicious. We ought to turn back and search for him."
Furthermore, he spoke thus:

"Yet that noble one possesses great majestic power; since he was able to survive by means of the perils of the great ocean, how could he fail to reach a place on level ground where there are no obstacles?"
Having spoken these words, he immediately set out on his journey.
At that time, Saṃgharakṣita was sleeping upon the sandy desert; scorched by the sun, he woke up.
Rising and looking in all directions, he saw no one at all, and he spoke these words:
"These caravan leaders have abandoned me and departed.
I cannot remain here; it is best that I proceed further.

He then traveled by stages; finding no human tracks but only a narrow path, he followed it until he reached a great forest. Within it, he saw a monastery, magnificent and exquisite, with couches, seats, mats, rugs, and carpets, and with halls, pavilions, and windows of extraordinary beauty.
Within it there were also flowing springs and clear ponds, with rows of jewel trees whose wondrous and variegated branches and leaves cast shifting shadows.
In those pools there were also various birds—white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, white geese, and other such birds—making it resemble a celestial palace.
In this monastery there were several bhikṣus who were fully endowed with dignified deportment.
At that time, Saṃgharakṣita, seeing his fellow practitioners of the holy life, went to them and paid them respectful homage by prostrating at their feet.
That bhikṣu said: "Welcome, welcome, Saṅgharakṣita!"
"From where have you come?
Saṃgharakṣita answered with all the details as related above.
Then that bhikṣu, having had him rest and settle himself, led him into the monastery, where he saw various fine seats and exquisite food and drink.
The bhikṣu asked,
"Are you hungry and thirsty? He replied:
“[The child] cried out,
‘I am hungry and thirsty. [The mother] replied, ‘If you are hungry, eat.’”
He replied, "I shall eat together with you once we have waited for the Sangha's meal.
The bhikṣu reported this, saying:
"You are weary from the road; you should eat for now.
If you wait until mealtime, there will be various difficulties.
After Saṃgharakṣita had finished eating, he moved to one side and sat down.
When the time for the meal arrived, the *ghanṭā* was struck and the Saṃgha assembled; each carrying their own bowl, they went to the dining hall and sat down in order.

At that moment, the monastery vanished, and their bowls were transformed into iron clubs. Each used these clubs to strike one another, until their heads and faces were shattered and blood flowed across the ground, as they endured various forms of intense suffering.
When the time for the meal had passed, the monastery reappeared; the bhikṣus were restored to their former state, their faculties serene as they sat in orderly rows.
At that time, Saṃgharakṣita went to the place where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Noble ones!..."
"What causes and karmic actions did I commit such that this has happened, and I must undergo these various sufferings?
He replied: "Venerable Saṃgharakṣita!"
"The people of this Jambudvīpa have no faith.
Saṃgharakṣita replied, "I see it with my own eyes right now; why do they not believe?"
He said, "Saṃgharakṣita!
In the past, we were śrāvakas under the Buddha Kāśyapa; when it was time for our meal, we would fight and strike one another."
"Because of this karma, I have been made to undergo these minor sufferings in this separate hell;
when my life here ends, I shall fall into the great hells.
You should now go and inform the Saṃgha of Jambudvīpa that at every mealtime they must not fight or strike one another."
"If one fights and strikes others, one will surely encounter this suffering.
Saṃgharakṣita replied, "Indeed, it is so."
He then took his leave and departed.
As he proceeded by stages, he again saw a monastery;
its magnificence was no different from the previous one, and he likewise saw a bhikṣu whose deportment was perfectly complete, until, as before, they vanished from sight.

In the alms bowls of the bhikṣus, there was molten copper, and they were dousing one another with it; this continued until the monastery appeared, whereupon the community of bhikṣus sat down in their proper order.
Saṃgharakṣita said, "Venerable Sir!..."
"By the power of what karma have you come to this place to undergo such suffering?
The bhikṣu replied, "Sentient beings are difficult to inspire with faith."
He replied, "I have seen it with my own eyes; how could I not believe it?
[The Buddha said,] "Saṃgharakṣita, you should know that I was a śrāvaka under the Buddha Kāśyapa."
Whenever it was time for a meal, we would obtain various superior and exquisite foods, such as fine clarified butter.
At that time, when there were guest bhikṣus present, we, being stingy with our food, would think:
"We shall wait until those guests have departed, and then we will eat together."

At that time, it happened that it rained for seven days; because of the mud and rain, the guests were unable to proceed on their journey. Consequently, they did not travel for seven days and did not consume this food, which had all become putrid and unfit for offering, so they took it and discarded it.
Because they received offerings from the faithful but ate unequally and immediately cast them away,
by virtue of this karma, they are born into a separate hell where they undergo slight suffering;
having finished that experience, they pass away and fall into the great hells.
He said, "Saṃgharakṣita!
Inform the bhikṣus among humans that they must not do such a thing."
"If that were so, you would surely be summoned to suffer the torments of the great hells.
Having heard these words, he took his leave and departed.
Traveling on by stages, he saw another monastery, as magnificent and beautiful as the previous one, where there were many bhikṣus.
Seeing that the time for the meal had arrived, they sat down as before.
Suddenly, a fire broke out in the monastery, its fierce flames blazing intensely.
The entire assembly of bhikṣus was completely consumed by the fire.
When the time for the meal had passed, the monastery returned to its former state.
The assembly of bhikṣus, their faculties well-disciplined, sat down in order.
Saṃgharakṣita questioned and answered them as before.
He said: "Listen well.

In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was a śrāvaka; however, I broke the precepts, and the Saṃgha expelled me. Consequently, I went to another place and lived together with those of a similar nature."
Later, at another time, there was a bhikṣu who maintained the precepts with diligence and came to this place.
Again, at another time, there was yet another bhikṣu whose observance of the precepts was without flaw.
They also came to this place, where they disciplined the monastic community and rebuked us; consequently, we became unable to endure it.
Later, at another time when it was mealtime and the great assembly wished to eat, we then united our hearts to set fire to the monastery until it was completely consumed by flames.
"By the power of that karma, you have come to be born here and must first undergo these specific sufferings;
once these are exhausted, you shall fall into the great hells.
You should report this to the bhikṣu of Jambudvīpa."
"Do not do this. If you do so, you will likewise undergo such suffering as we do.
Furthermore, he saw other sentient beings whose bodies were like walls, or like great trees, or like leaves, or like flowers, or like fruits, or even like pillars.
"These sentient beings are all bound together with ropes; pull them until they are severed.
At that time, Saṃgharakṣita proceeded gradually forward until he reached a dwelling place.
There were five hundred ṛṣis who, seeing Saṃgharakṣita approaching, said to one another:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, is a man of many words and much talk; you should not converse with him.
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, Saṃgharakṣita arrived there and said to the sages, "You should provide me with a place to stay.
The sages remained silent; no one spoke with him.
Among the assembly was a certain seer who, out of compassion and pity, addressed the other seers, saying:
"Have you not provided lodging for the śramaṇa Śākyaputras? The seers replied:
"You should grant him a seat, but do not engage him in conversation.
Saṃgharakṣita replied, "Very well."
He settled Saṃgharakṣita in an empty room, washed his feet, and prepared a seat.
Having arranged the seat, he sat upright with right mindfulness.
Previously, there had been many celestial maidens dwelling in the hermitage; at the first watch of the night, they came to Saṃgharakṣita and said to him:
“Noble One! We pray that you will explain the essential points of the Dharma to us.
Saṃgharakṣita replied:
"Sisters! You all enjoy great happiness.
I was restrained by the sages and forbidden from speaking; it is for this reason that I have been able to dwell in this quiet chamber."
"Sisters, did you send me to preach the Dharma, wishing for me to leave?
At that time, the goddesses thought to themselves:
"This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has come from afar; his body must be weary, so we should let him go for now."
Having had this thought, the devas departed.
After midnight had passed, the celestial maiden returned and went to Saṃgharakṣita, saying:
"Noble One!..."
"Please preach the Dharma for me.
Saṃgharakṣita replied,
"Are you certain that I am to be expelled from this place?"
The devas thought again:
"He has not yet had enough sleep; we should depart for now.
During the latter part of the night, the celestial maidens returned and went to Saṃgharakṣita, saying to him:
“Noble One! Please teach me the Dharma.
Saṃgharakṣita replied again:
"Sister! Do you wish for me to leave this place?
The goddess replied:
"Now that dawn has broken, why do you not depart?
Have you perhaps not heard the Buddha say:
'When one arrives at a place of great terror, one must practice patience'?"
"Is that so? At that time, Saṃgharakṣita thought to himself:
"The celestial maiden is weary of me; I should depart quickly."
He further thought:
"These seers are all followers of heterodox teachings; I should recite the verses they study so that those who hear them will all be filled with joy."
Having formed this thought, he then spoke these verses:
"Nakedness and long hair, Smearing ashes and fasting,
Sleeping on the ground and bathing the body, Crouching and perverse thoughts;”
These various false dharmas will ultimately not exempt one from birth and death;
only by means of the true and wondrous Dharma can one adorn oneself.
Abiding in right view and dwelling in reflection, one should sever greed, hatred, and the like.
Practicing compassion, joy, and equanimity, with the life-force of sentient beings unbroken;
diligently training in the precepts— this is the true śramaṇa,
this is also the brāhmaṇa, and this is the nature of a great bhikṣu.
When these verses were spoken, the seers, having heard them, said to one another,
"This one recites our scriptures.
Thereupon, the assembly of seers each rose up in private and listened silently to his words.
Because the celestial maidens were infatuated with that rishi, they could not see one another.
At that time, Saṃgharakṣita preached the *Nagaropama-sūtra* (The Discourse on the Simile of the City) for them, causing them to attain awakening.
When he had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of seers realized the third fruit of the path.
The celestial maidens caused those seers to regain their original minds, so that they were able to see one another; with one voice, they proclaimed:
"Well said! Well said!"
"This sutra is subtle and wondrous.
Having offered this praise, they addressed one another, saying:
"Did you all come from there to listen to the Dharma?"
He replied, "Yes. He spoke again:
"I have now obtained a sublime and excellent benefit here.
Then the assembly of sages all addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!..."
"May we also go forth and receive full ordination to practice the holy life,
just as the Venerable Ones do. Saṃgharakṣita replied, "O venerable ones!"
That you are able to possess such superior faith is a virtuous matter.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"Those who are able to leave the household life obtain five kinds of benefit."
What are the five?
First, the merit of renouncing the household life is my own personal benefit and is not shared with others; therefore, the wise should seek renunciation.

Second, one should know for oneself that one was formerly a person of low station who was driven by others; yet after leaving the household life, one receives offerings, prostrations, and praise from others. For this reason, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Third, when life ends here, one shall be reborn in the heavens and leave the three evil realms; for this reason, the wise should seek to go forth from the household life.

Fourth, by relinquishing worldly attachments, one departs from birth and death and shall attain the secure, unsurpassed nirvana; for this reason, the wise should seek to go forth from the household life.
"Fifth, one will always be praised by all Buddhas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all superior persons; for this reason, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
You should contemplate these benefits and, with a sincere mind, cast off the worldly snares to seek great merit."
Therefore, I now ordain you and let you leave the household life.
Do you wish to leave the household life here,
or rather under the Buddha?
The sages replied,
“We wish to go with the Venerable One to the presence of the Buddha and there go forth from the household life.
The sages further said:
"Are we going by means of the Venerable One's supernatural power,
or shall we go by means of our own supernormal faculties?
Upon hearing these words, Saṃgharakṣita was displeased and thought to himself:
"The assembly of seers, upon hearing my exposition of the Dharma, attained the fruits of the Path;
though I have explained it, I have not attained such fruits.
He said to the seers:
"Wait a short while; I have something to do.
He went beneath a tree, spread his seat there, and sat down cross-legged with his body upright and his mindfulness established, his mind serene.
He further thought:
"The Buddha has taught that there are five benefits of extensive learning, as explained at length elsewhere.

Through such diligence, his afflictions were suddenly severed, and he subsequently attained the fruit of Arhatship. Having transcended the three realms, he felt neither anger nor resentment whether his body was cut with a blade or smeared with fragrant paste; he viewed gold and earth as equal, without distinction, and became worthy of being venerated by Śakra, the various devas, Brahmā, and others.
He then said to the seer,
"Grasp the hem of my robe and, sustained by my supernatural power, go to the place where the Buddha is.
Immediately they ascended into the void, like a king of geese or like a hawk or a falcon.
The five hundred merchants had not yet arrived; they each halted their saddles and pack animals, and seeing Saṃgharakṣita from afar, addressed him, saying:
"Noble One! Welcome to your arrival. Where do you intend to go now?"
He replied, "These five hundred rishis wish to seek ordination under the Buddha.
I am now accompanying them to bring them to the Buddha's presence."
Then the five hundred merchants all said to him:
"Noble One! We wish to go forth together with you."
He spoke again:
"Noble One! Please descend and stay here."
"Wait a moment while we entrust our various possessions to our families; then we shall go together with you.
Having made these arrangements, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita went to the Buddha's presence together with those thousand people.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was preaching the Dharma while surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of hundreds of thousands.
Seeing Saṃgharakṣita and his companions approaching from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"Do you all see this bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita coming along, preceded and followed by those thousand people?"
The bhikṣus replied, “We all saw it.
The World-Honored One said:
"There is no offering to the world greater than this: to transform people so that they leave the household life, and to discipline and deliver them.
Then Saṃgharakṣita and the others all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Venerable Saṅgharakṣita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These clansmen, numbering one thousand, all desire to go forth under the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha and receive full ordination, so as to become bhikṣus.”
“May the Buddha, out of his compassion, take pity on us and grant us permission.
The Buddha said, “Welcome, bhikṣus!”
"Within my Dharma, you have well cultivated the holy life and become a great śramaṇa.

As soon as these words were spoken, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the saṃghāṭī robes naturally appeared upon his body. His head appeared as if it had been shaved for seven days; with a flask and bowl in hand, his majestic deportment was complete like that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing, as described at length elsewhere.
The World-Honored One instructed and exhorted them according to the Dharma;

each applied themselves with diligence, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship, becoming free from the desires of the three realms. This is explained at length until it is said that even Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to make offerings to them.
At that time, the Venerable Saṅgharakṣita addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In that place, I saw various sentient beings whose forms were like walls, or like pillars and trees, or like leaves, flowers, and fruits, or like brooms, cauldrons, ladles, and mortars."
"What kind of karma must he have performed in his previous life to receive such a retribution?
The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita:

"In general, for all sentient beings, the karma they themselves create must be experienced by themselves; others cannot take their place. This is explained at length until it is said that the fruit and retribution must likewise be experienced by oneself."
In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Buddha, residing at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, all the novices (śrāmaṇera) belonging to that Buddha were reborn as bhikṣus. Saṃgharakṣita!
As for those forms you saw that resembled walls, those sentient beings had smeared the walls of the saṃgha with mud; therefore, they received such a retribution.
As for those things that appear like pillars, those sentient beings previously defiled monastic pillars with snot and saliva;
due to that karma, they undergo such retribution.

As for the one whose form was like a ladle: he had formerly been a *śrāmaṇera* who, while serving honey-water among the Saṃgha, had a guest bhikṣu arrive at his place; the *śrāmaṇera* was then washing the ladle.
The visiting bhikṣu asked,
"Is non-timely juice being distributed among the Saṃgha?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"The distribution of the drinks is finished.
Do you not see that I am now washing the ladles?
he said, and then gave rise to anger and abuse.
Due to the power of that karma, they receive such retribution.
As for the one you see whose form resembles a mortar, he was once a bhikṣu in a past life who, while intending to have an alms bowl made, had a śrāmaṇera in charge of the Saṃgha’s storehouse.
The bhikṣu who was making the bowl went to the śrāmaṇera and borrowed it,
saying, "I shall use it for pounding. Then the śrāmaṇera said:
“Venerable sir!
Please wait a short while; I am currently quite busy.
After a short time, he gave him the mortar.
The bhikṣu immediately gave rise to anger and spoke these harsh words:
"If I were my own master, I would not merely borrow a mortar to pound sesame seeds; I would pound your body as well!
At that time, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"If I were to retaliate, he would surely become even more enraged. He remained silent.
Knowing that the bhikṣu’s anger had subsided and his mind was settled, the śrāmaṇera then went to him and said:
"Do you now know what kind of person I am?
The Venerable replied,
"You were a śrāmaṇera who went forth under the teachings of Kāśyapa Buddha."
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"As for your matter of leaving the household life, what you have done is not yet accomplished.
You are bound by all the afflictions, whereas I have attained liberation."
"You have uttered coarse words; you must confess and repent them, and your transgression shall then be diminished and purified.
He immediately confessed and repented, and consequently was reborn with the body of a mortar.
As for the one whose form you see resembling a cauldron, in the past he served as a *śuddhakarman* (pure man) for a monastery, attending to the bhikṣus and boiling medicine for them.
At that time, the bhikṣu was angry, and because of this, the attendant (kappiyakāraka) gave rise to resentment and intentionally struck the cauldron until it broke.
Due to the power of this karma, his body became shaped like the cauldron.

As for what you saw regarding those who tied them with ropes and pulled them until they snapped: in the past, he served as the *karmadāna*. When there were external offerings, he was to ensure that the Saṃgha made use of them according to the seasons, whether it was cold or hot.

However, at that time, the *karmadāna* diverted the clothing and goods intended for the summer months to use during winter, and diverted the clothing and goods intended for winter to use during the heat.
"Because of this karma, he undergoes such suffering.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and reported the matter to the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Saṅgharakṣita!"
"What kind of karma did he perform?

By what karma was he born into the family of a great wealthy householder, and furthermore, how did he leave the household life to realize the fruit of arhatship and perform such great deeds of benefit?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should listen. The meritorious deeds performed by the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, up until his own experiencing of their results, are as described at length above."
In the distant past, when the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
At that time, the Buddha Kāśyapa was staying at Rṣipatana in the Deer Park, and Saṃgharakṣita also went forth as a monk there.
He was the leader of a large group and had five hundred disciples; men and women from all directions placed their full trust and faith in him.
At that time, this leader of the group maintained the pure conduct (brahmacarya) with steadfastness until the end of his life, without any lapse or transgression, yet he gained nothing thereby.
Later, as he was about to pass away, he uttered these words:
"I have practiced the holy life within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya of Kāśyapa Buddha with diligence and without slackness, yet I have not attained any extraordinary or superior fruit."

May all these merits serve as a support for us, so that in a future age when Śākyamuni Buddha appears in the world, we may go forth into homelessness within his Dharma and Vinaya, purely cultivate the holy life, sever all afflictions, and realize the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, five hundred disciples came to their teacher’s place and said,
“Upādhyāya, have you attained the supreme fruit?”
The teacher said,
"Not yet. He spoke to the teacher again, saying:
"What kind of supreme vows have you made?
The Master replied,
"I have made the aforementioned vows."
The disciples all said together:
"If our Upādhyāya has realized such a fruit,
we too shall follow him into the homeless life and likewise realize the fruit of Arhatship."
At that time, more than five hundred people from a village came to the teacher’s place; after the same exchange of questions and answers as before, he spoke at length until:
"We, too, wish to realize the fruit of arhatship."
"O bhikṣus! Do not harbor any other thoughts.
Who else could that leader of the assembly in the past have been?"
The one who was Saṃgharakṣita is this very person here.
Those who were the five hundred disciples in the past are these five hundred sages.
Those who were the five hundred people from the village in the past are the present caravan leader and his companions.
Because he formerly made offerings to the Saṃgha as its leader, by virtue of that karma, he was born into the family of a great wealthy householder.
Furthermore, due to his aspiration, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Furthermore, because he was extensively able to discipline others in the past, in this life he again succeeds in disciplining many people, widely delivering sentient beings for their benefit. You bhikṣus!
If one plants white karma, one will receive a white retribution; this applies likewise to mixed karma and so forth, as explained in detail above.
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and reported the matter to the Buddha, saying:
"In what place did the bhikṣu who was formerly a transformed nāga first give rise to the thought of enlightenment?"
The Buddha said:

"In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa... [as extensively described] ...in the Śrāvastī Deer Park, he preached the essential Dharma to his śrāvakas: 'O bhikṣus!'"

One should sit upright with right mindfulness in a state of tranquility within an araṇya, among the mountains, beneath a tree, in a secluded charnel ground, in a grass hut in a remote area, or in a cave or grotto.
"You should apply yourselves with diligent effort and not be negligent.
You should act according to my instructions; you must train yourselves in this way.

When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they followed the Buddha’s teaching: some went to Mount Sumeru, some headed toward Lake Anavatapta, and some went to other lakes; among them were those who went to the Seven Golden Mountains, and some remained in cities and villages.

At that time, there was a dragon who, not long after being born, was seized by the King of the Golden-Winged Birds and carried into the air. Looking down, he saw a bhikṣu sitting upright in meditative concentration with his faculties perfectly tranquil. The dragon thought to himself:
"These bhikṣus are in a state of profound peace and happiness; they are not like me, who must endure such suffering."
He then conceived a profound sense of devotion and earnest faith; having formed this thought, he passed away.

In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a brahmin who possessed the sixfold qualities. [The deceased] was born into that family and grew up there, whereupon he went forth under the Buddha, received full ordination, and diligently cultivated the holy life. Having severed all afflictions, he realized the fruit of arhatship, until even Śakra and the various devas came to make offerings to him.
He immediately observed for himself: "By what karma did this come about?
From where did I pass away to be born here, and how was such a fruit obtained?
He then perceived that he had passed away from the realm of nāgas to be born among humans, and further saw that he had conceived a heart of profound devotion toward a great śrāvaka.

Furthermore, seeing that his parents were in that dragon palace during his past life as a dragon, he immediately manifested supernatural powers and went to the dragon palace, where he saw his former parents weeping in grief and distress.
He asked the dragon,
"For what reason are you weeping?
The dragon replied:
“O Noble One! I gave birth to a son, but before long, he was seized by the King of the Golden-Winged Birds and taken away; we do not know his whereabouts.
She replied to her mother, saying:

"I am your beloved son; having passed away from this life, I was born into a brahmin family. Furthermore, under the guidance of Kāśyapa Buddha, I went forth into homelessness, diligently cultivated the holy life, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of arhatship."
The mother of the nāga said:
"O Noble One! This is indeed difficult to believe and is also most extraordinary."
"However, my beloved son was of an extremely evil nature; it was impossible for him even to be born in a happy realm, let alone attain the state of an Arhat.
He then replied to his mother, "I have truly realized the fruit; these are not empty words."
The mother of the nāga said,
"If it be as you say, from this day forward, please accept food for me every single day.
He then accepted her request by remaining silent.
The bhikṣu regularly partook of various foods of superior flavor every day, and having finished his meal, he would return to his own residence.
Now, that bhikṣu had a śrāmaṇera, and at one time the bhikṣus asked the śrāmaṇera:
"Where does your preceptor go to eat each day before returning?"
The śrāmaṇera replied, "I do not know either. The bhikṣu said:
"Your teacher partakes daily of various kinds of food and drink;
why do you not go [to him]? He replied:
"My preceptor possesses great majestic power and was able to go for food;
I have no such power, so how could I go on my own? The bhikṣu replied:
"Your teacher wishes to depart; you should silently grasp the corner of his *cīvara*.
The novice replied, "I do not decline to grasp it, but I fear he might fall to the ground."
The bhikṣu replied, "Your teacher’s robe remains tied to Mount Sumeru and does not fall; how much less so would your own body.
Having been thus exhorted, when it was time for the meal, he went silently to his teacher's location and stood in a secluded spot.
When the master wished to ascend into the air and depart, the śrāmaṇera grasped the corner of his master’s robe and likewise ascended into the air.
At that time, within the dragon palace, two seats and two maṇḍalas were prepared.
Having seen this, the Master asked the nāgas,
"For what reason have you set out these two seats upon the altar?
At that time, the nāgas replied:
"Should you look behind to see if there is anyone else?
The Master then turned his head and saw this novice: "Have you also come?"
He replied, “Yes. The teacher said:
"Excellent. Having arrived and taken his seat there, the nāgas thought:
"This master of ours has attained a sublime fruit; he possesses great majesty and virtue, and is worthy of divine food."
"However, since that disciple has not yet attained such [realization], he should be given ordinary food.
Having formed this thought, the nāgas provided offerings according to his intention.

When the meal was finished, the śrāmaṇera took his preceptor’s bowl; in that bowl there remained a single grain of rice, which the śrāmaṇera took and ate. That rice was sweet and delicious, its flavor beyond compare in the world.
After the śrāmaṇera had finished eating, he thought to himself:
"The two of them eat together, yet they act as if they were two different kinds of people.
A feeling of resentment arose in his heart, and he made this vow:
"I went forth under the Buddha Kāśyapa and practiced the holy life.
By the merit of this, I vow to obtain a dragon body of great majesty and power, seize this palace, and drive out all the other dragons."

Having made this vow with such fierce resentment that he disregarded even his own life, clear water began to flow from both his hands, causing all the nāgas within the palace to suffer from headaches.
The nāgas said: "Venerable One!
However, this śrāmaṇera does not attend to wholesome matters; he ought to be restrained."
The preceptor said: "This is a miserable realm.
For what reason do you now give rise to such a thought?"
At that time, the śrāmaṇera replied to his preceptor with a verse:
"My mind has already gone far away; it is difficult to pursue and retrieve.
Why is it so difficult to repent?"
"The water from both hands has already flowed.
Having spoken this verse, the novice became a nāga and immediately expelled the various nāga kings, taking up residence within the palace himself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣu who was the transformed nāga is this very nāga king who has been expelled.
It was at that time that the nāga king first gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; this was his beginning."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, some non-Buddhist outsiders went to Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park and saw the dwellings of the bhikṣus, including their beds, seats, mats, bedding, requisites for use, and various foods and drinks. They then thought:
"The food, drink, bedding, and requisites used by these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are excellent."
Nevertheless, the Dharma is not like me.
You should leave the household life here and enjoy the requisites of food, drink, and bedding here;
if you wish to hear the Dharma, you should go to that place.
Having had this thought, he immediately went to the place where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Noble ones! I wish to go forth."
That community of bhikṣus then granted him the going-forth and the full ordination.
It was the constant custom of the non-Buddhists to perform the poṣadha on the fourteenth day,
whereas for the bhikṣus it was on the fifteenth day.
When the fourteenth day arrived, those non-Buddhists went to their own non-Buddhist quarters to perform the *poṣadha*;
on the fifteenth day, they again performed the *poṣadha* in the presence of the *bhikṣus*.
Later, at another time, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight during the *poṣadha* ceremony of the Saṃgha, the non-Buddhists thought to themselves:
"Since the *poṣadha* is being held in both places today, shall we go to that location?"
"Is it for this reason? He further thought:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, possess hearts of loving-kindness and compassion; their Dharma is broad and relaxed."
"The rules of those non-Buddhists are strict and severe.
If I do not go, they will surely punish me heavily and rebuke me with anger.
Having thought this, he went to visit them.
Then the bhikṣus struck the ghaṇṭā and assembled the saṃgha.
Once the great assembly had gathered, the presiding officer addressed them, saying:
"Has the entire saṃgha assembled?"
The community of bhikṣus did not see that outsider bhikṣu;
having failed to see him, they performed the *poṣadha*.
When the following day arrived, he returned.
The bhikṣus asked, "Where did you go yesterday? He replied:
"I shall go to and come from this place of the holy life," he said; furthermore,
"I shall enjoy food, drink, and bedding here, yet the Dharma received shall remain in my original place."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Those non-Buddhists cling to what is false; their minds take pleasure in those teachings, and they do not abandon their wrong views."
"However, such a person brings no benefit to my teaching and cannot increase the eye of Dharma; they must be expelled and sent back to lay life.
From this day forward, when anyone comes seeking ordination, a bhikṣu should ask:
'Are you not a non-Buddhist, nor one who delights in heterodox teachings?'"
If he says, "Yes," he must be expelled.
"If one does not ask, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Whenever one should ordain a non-Buddhist who ought to be expelled, what kind of non-Buddhist should be expelled?
The Buddha said:
"First, those who wear the robes of non-Buddhists; second, those whose hearts delight in their views; third, those who return to and adhere to their original garb."
The Sūtra clarifies that when the dawn appears, these three types of persons must all be expelled through the rite of *parivāsa*.
This occurred in the city of Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, gave birth to a son, whom he nourished with milk and food.
At that time, the elder said to his wife:
"O virtuous lady!
Although this son has used my wealth, he will also be able to repay all my debts on my behalf."
Having spoken these words, he took his goods and traveled abroad to engage in trade for profit, whereupon he perished and failed to return.
His wife, relying on her own strength and seeking the aid of her relatives, raised him through various means until he gradually grew up.
At that time, this boy went along with the other youths to the house of another elder.
At that moment, the elder had a young daughter who, upon seeing the boy, threw a flower garland at him.
Then the youths asked,
"Do you have an appointment with this woman? He replied:
"Yes," the boys replied, "this elder is stern and ill-tempered by nature; do not do this thing, lest it bring harm upon you."
The other boys guarded this boy until sunset so that he would not engage in unrighteous acts, and then they accompanied him together to his mother’s place.
They reported privately to his mother, saying:
“This young boy wishes to commit an unrighteous act with the daughter of such-and-such an elder.”
"We have already exhorted him and restrained him from doing so.
We shall now return; it is fitting that you should prevent him during this night.
The mother said:
"You have done a most excellent thing in being able to exhort one another thus.

Her mother then had the boy enter the room and settle him there; she further placed a water-pitcher and a washbasin within the room, and the mother herself laid down upon a bed positioned right at the doorway.
After midnight had passed, the son said to his mother, "Open the door for me;
I wish to go outside and relieve myself.
His mother then replied:
"The chamber has already been provided with a washbasin;
you may now attend to your needs. After a short while, the son spoke again:
"Open the door for me."
The mother did not open it either, so the son became enraged.
The mother said,
"The place where you are going, I already knew beforehand."
"I would rather die here than ever open the door for you.

Driven by the fires of passion, he committed no evil and felt no aversion to sinful karma; thus, at that moment, he drew his sword, killed his mother, cast her corpse upon the ground, and immediately went to the house of the elder.
Having arrived there, he saw the young woman, her body trembling;
she said, "Do not be afraid; I dwell here alone, and there is no one else."
The youth thought to himself,
"I must now inform him that I have already killed my mother," and he said:
“O maiden! I have already taken the life-force of your mother.
The girl said:
"Is she your biological mother,
or is she your wet nurse? He replied:
"This is my mother who gave birth to me.
The woman thought to herself, "If this man,
in his rage, would even kill his own mother, how much more so would he kill someone like me?"
Having had this thought, he replied, "You should wait a moment;
I shall ascend to the upper story for a short while.
Once the woman had gone up to the upper story, he called out in a loud voice:
"There is a thief here!
Having heard this, the man slipped out through a drainage pipe and,
upon reaching his own home, threw the sword to the ground and cried out in a loud voice:
"The bandits have killed my mother!
The bandits have killed my mother!
Having uttered these words, he then performed the cremation and burial of his mother according to the worldly custom.
He reflected within himself:
"I am truly an evil person who has committed the gravest of transgressions.
His heart was filled with trembling fear, finding no peace; he then went to various shrines to worship the gods, seeking answers from them everywhere.
"What karmic practices should one cultivate to extinguish grave offenses? Some replied,
"One should enter the fire."
Some said: "I threw myself from a high cliff. Others said: [...]"I threw myself from a high cliff. Some said:
"Cast oneself into the water," or some might say:
"Hang one's own body."
Each of them spoke of the means they had employed, all intended to cause his death and leaving him no way out.
Later, when they went to the Jetavana Grove, they saw a bhikṣu reciting a sūtra and śāstra, in which the verse said:
"If a person commits evil deeds, / Cultivating goodness can extinguish them."
"He can illuminate the world, like the sun emerging from the clouds.
At that time, this person thought to himself:
"The renunciant disciples of the Śākya have a method for removing transgressions; I should now go forth as a monk, cultivate various wholesome deeds, and thereby extinguish my sins."
He immediately went to the place where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Noble ones! I wish to go forth; I pray that you will have compassion for me."
Then that bhikṣu granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination upon him.

Having gone forth, he applied himself with diligence to recitation and study, until he attained complete mastery of the teachings of the Tripiṭaka; his eloquence was unimpeded, and he was skilled in debate and response.
Another bhikṣu asked that person: "Venerable one!
For what reason do you practice such arduous asceticism with such diligence?"
"What else do you seek?
That person replied,
"I do so for the sake of eliminating my grave offenses."
He asked, "What offense have you committed? He replied:
"Kill your mother.
He asked again,
"Is it your biological mother?"
"Is she the wet nurse?
He replied, "She is the biological mother."
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If a person who has killed his mother seeks to go forth from home, granting him the going-forth would destroy my Dharma; he must be expelled immediately."
From this day forward, within my Dharma and Vinaya, if anyone comes seeking to go forth, you must ask them:
"Are you not one who has killed their mother?"
"If you do not inquire [about this], you shall incur an offense against the Dharma.
Once that person had been expelled by the assembly, he thought to himself:
"I must not return to secular life; I ought to go far away to dwell in a remote border region."
He then went to a border region and transformed himself into a householder. This householder conceived faith and reverence for the bhikṣu and built a monastery for him.
Travelers from all directions came to this monastery; to everyone who arrived, he preached the Dharma, and many realized the fruit of arhatship.
Again, at another time, his body became afflicted by illness; though he treated it with various medicinal roots, fruits, stalks, leaves, and diverse herbs, it was not cured.
He gradually grew more debilitated, and his remaining life was but short.
He told his disciples,
"You should construct a bathhouse.
At that time, the disciples followed his instructions and proceeded to build the bathhouse.
At that time, the teacher spoke these verses:
"All accumulations come to an end; All that is lofty must fall;
All meetings end in separation; All who have life return to death."
Having spoken this verse, he immediately passed away and fell into the Avīci Hell.
However, those disciples who had realized arhatship entered meditative concentration and observed with discernment: "Where has our preceptor been reborn?"
He scrutinized the palaces of the various devas but did not see him;
he further examined the human realm, the animal realm, and among the hungry ghosts, yet saw him nowhere.
He then examined the hells and beheld him within the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the disciples thought to themselves:
"While our Upādhyāya was alive, he maintained the precepts and possessed great learning, and he sustained us by means of the Dharma."
"What karma did he commit to fall into the Avīci Hell?
Upon further careful observation, he saw it was the karma of killing his mother.
As he was tormented by the fierce fires of hell, he thought they were the bathhouse he had built, and so he cried out:
"The sauna! The sauna! The blazing, fierce fire burns me intensely!
At that moment, the wardens at the gate struck him on the head with clubs and said:
"This person of meager merit and sinful karma—this is the Avīci Hell; how can you say it is a bathhouse?
When his head was struck, he gave rise to a virtuous mind and immediately passed away, being reborn in the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Whenever one is born in the heavens, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I come?
Where am I born now?"
Furthermore, by what karma was this caused?

When I gave rise to this thought, I saw that after dying from the Avīci Hell, I was born in the palace of the Four Great Heavenly Kings; it was because I had provided a bathhouse for the bhikṣus to bathe that, through the power of this merit, I was born in this heaven.
At that time, the deva-son again thought to himself:
"It is because of the World-Honored One’s skillful means that I have been born in the heavens.
I should not remain here complacently; I must go to the presence of the World-Honored One to repay this kindness."
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and heard the sublime Dharma, he immediately realized the first fruit of the path.
Once he had attained the vision of the Truths, he returned to his celestial palace.
At that time, his principal disciple—an Arhat—was seated in the place of honor when the assembly was about to eat.

A junior disciple was serving water for the saṃgha; at that time, as the senior monk received the water into his bowl, the tip of his finger touched the water and he perceived it to be extremely cold, whereupon he thought:
"I shall now drink this cold water here."
"My preceptor is drinking molten copper within the hells.
He then surveyed the hells but saw him nowhere;
he further surveyed the realms of humans, animals, and hungry ghosts, yet saw him in none of them.

He immediately looked toward the heavens and saw that [the deceased] had been reborn in the palace of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, where he had further realized the first fruit of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha.
Having seen this, he smiled and said:
"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—these great, pure, and wondrous matters are inconceivable."
"This is an extremely grave karma that leads to rebirth in hell;
yet it possesses a superior efficacy that allows for rebirth in the heavens.
The water-carrier said to the Venerable One:
“Did you smile with joy because your preceptor died and you attained the position of senior monk?
He replied, “Venerable one!...”
"What you have asked now is not the proper time;
when the Saṃgha has assembled, you may ask about this matter, and I shall explain it to you.
Later, at another time, the community of bhikṣus assembled.
Among his junior fellow students, someone asked,
"Virtuous One!
What did you see previously that caused you to smile with such joy?"
“Did you laugh out of joy because you saw that your upādhyāya had died and thus become the senior elder?
At that time, the leader of the assembly related the matter in detail to the Saṃgha as previously described. Then all the disciples were filled with great joy and all exclaimed:
“The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha brings great benefit; though our upādhyāya committed such karmic offenses, he has attained rebirth in heaven.”
"Killing one's father is likewise a transgression against the natural order (*ānantarya*)," as was explained at length previously.

At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma for the king. When King Prasenajit realized the Truth (*satyadarśana*), eighty thousand celestial beings simultaneously attained realization, along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of brahmins, *vānaprasthas*, and householders.
At that time, King Śrīghoṣa beat the drum and issued a proclamation, saying:
"Those who dwell within the borders of my kingdom must not commit theft.
Should anyone be guilty of theft, they shall be sentenced to death."
"To those whose property has been stolen, I shall personally provide goods to compensate for their value.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had further delivered the *Kumāra-sūtra* to subdue the king, the king again beat the drum and issued a proclamation, saying:
"Within the borders of my kingdom, no one shall commit theft."
"If anyone commits this offense, they shall be sentenced to death.
As for the family whose property was stolen, I shall restore it from my own treasury.

At that time, there were bandits in the kingdom of Magadha who came toward the kingdom of Kośala; in the border region between the two kingdoms, all merchants passing to and fro were robbed of their goods.
At that time, merchants from the kingdom of Magadha were traveling together toward the kingdom of Kośala, and they said to one another:
"In these two regions there are many bandits, and they also demand heavy taxes."

At that time, most of the merchants turned back together, while only a small number proceeded forward. When they reached the middle of the road, a band of thieves rushed out and swiftly plundered them.
Among those merchants, some were killed, while others abandoned their wealth and fled.
Among the merchants was an arhat; having witnessed this event, while he was engaged in profound reflection, he was unwittingly deprived of his life-force by the bandits.
Those merchants who escaped by fleeing in different directions smeared their bodies with mud and went before King Prasenajit, wailing and crying out, and with palms joined, addressed the king:
"We were conducting trade within Your Majesty's realm when we were now plundered by bandits."
Then the king asked, "In which direction is it? He replied:
"In such-and-such a place.
The king then commanded his general named Virūḍhaka-Kāla to go there quickly, seize the thief, and bring him back.
Following these orders, the minister led the fourfold army to arrest them.
At that time, the bandits were staying in the thickets, dwelling there without fear and without wearing armor or mail, as they were in the midst of dividing the plundered wealth.
Vairocana and Garuḍa ordered their fourfold army to surround the bandits, and from all four sides they simultaneously beat drums and blew conch shells.
The bandits were terrified; they abandoned their belongings and fled, some being killed and others captured.
At that time, the Great General, having recovered the plundered goods and captured the thieves, went together to the King's presence and addressed the Great King, saying:
"These are the thieves along with their loot; they have now been apprehended."
The king said to the thief,
"I previously beat the drum and issued a proclamation:
'Within my kingdom, you shall not commit theft.'"
"If there be any who violate this, their lives shall be taken.
As for those whose homes have been plundered, I shall provide compensation from my own treasury.
The bandits said to the king:
"I have also heard the King beat the drum and proclaim an edict:
'Out of greed for wealth and goods, you disobeyed my command and went to steal.
" The King said:
"You are robbers; why do you take life?
They replied, "It is because we wish to cause fear in those before us."
The king said to them,
"You cause others to be terrified;
I shall now give you something never seen before to make you afraid."
The king commanded his ministers:
"Take this thief and execute him.
The ministers led the thief to a crossroads and announced to the crowd:
"This is a bandit; they intend to take him away to kill him.
As they were about to depart, one thief managed to escape and went to the Jeta Grove, where he approached a bhikṣu and said, "Noble One!..."
"I wish to leave the household life.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately granted him the going forth and full ordination.
All the other bandits were subsequently executed by the king.

Later, at another time, when the bhikṣus went to the charnel ground, the one who had been a bandit and had entered the order also came to the forest; seeing the king killing the bandits, tears fell from his eyes.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they said to one another,
"This newly ordained bhikṣu possesses such profound faith that he sheds tears from his eyes upon seeing this dead person."
Seeing the bhikṣu’s praise, she immediately let out a loud cry and wept bitterly.
The bhikṣu asked,
"For what reason do you weep so loudly?"
He replied, “This is my father; these are my elder and younger brothers.
He asked again:
"These bandits once killed an arhat;
have you also killed one? He replied:
“I once killed.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one kills an Arhat, this constitutes severing the field of merit and committing a heinous crime; it also destroys my Dharma. Such a person must be expelled and driven back to lay life."
"O bhikṣus! If anyone comes seeking to go forth, a bhikṣu should ask:
'Have you not killed an arhat?'"
"If one does not inquire [in this manner], one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there is another person who previously left the household life but later caused a schism in the Saṃgha, and subsequently comes again seeking to leave the household life, should he be granted ordination?"
The Buddha said, "It should not.
The Buddha then addressed Upāli:
"From this day forward, if anyone comes wishing to go forth, a bhikṣu should ask:
'Have you ever caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
If he has not, he should be ordained."
"If you do not inquire, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Furthermore, if there should be someone who, conceiving a malevolent and rebellious mind toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, causes the blood of the Buddha’s body to flow."
"If there is a person whose resolve seeks the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and whose mind delights in leaving the household life to practice the holy life (brahmacarya),
should such a person as this be granted ordination?
The Buddha said:
"No, it should not. If anyone comes seeking ordination, the bhikṣu should ask:
'Have you not, out of malice, shed the blood of a Buddha?'"
"If it is not so, they should be ordained.
If one does not inquire [in this manner], one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Furthermore, if there is a person who previously went forth as a monastic but, having committed any one of the four *pārājika* offenses, returned to lay life;
yet, regarding the wholesome Dharma, their heart still delights in going forth."
"Should they be delivered?
The Buddha said, "They should not."
If anyone comes seeking ordination as a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should ask:
"Have you ever committed one of the four pārājika offenses?
If he does not ask this, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who, having been formally charged for not seeing an offense, subsequently returns to the lay life."
If one returns to the household life and then goes forth again, or having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), commits various offenses yet refuses to confess them, saying,
"I do not see my offense," then the Saṃgha should carry out the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against him.
The Buddha said: "If,
after full ordination, a bhikṣu neither confesses nor abandons his evil views,
and the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension against him, he then returns to lay life."
"If one comes seeking to leave the household life but does not relinquish their original views, they must be expelled.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The disciples ordained by the group of six bhikṣus did not initially know the character and conduct of those six; they remained in dependence upon them.
Once they became aware of their evil nature, they all abandoned them and sought dependence elsewhere, yet they continued to inquire three times a day regarding their duties and activities.
At that time, the six bhikṣus said to one another:
"These black-bowl-born ones have snatched away the disciples we ourselves ordained;
if we ordain any more, we should ordain those of such a kind."
Later, at another time, Upānanda saw a man who was handless and said to him, "O worthy one!
For what reason do you not go forth into the homeless life now?"
He replied, "Who can deliver a person such as I,
who has no hands? Upānanda said:
“The Blessed One’s teaching is compassionate and forgiving;
I shall deliver them.
After he had received full ordination for three or five days and had been instructed in all matters of deportment, eating, and so forth, [the preceptor] then said to him:
“Have you not heard that deer do not raise deer?
Śrāvastī is very vast and spacious; you should go there to beg for food to support yourself.
The disciple replied:
"How can I go on alms-round now that I am like this? Upānanda replied,
"Venerable one!"

"I shall instruct you," he said, and immediately dressed him in all three robes, securing them with cords; he placed the alms bowl in a bag tied to his left arm and fastened the mendicant's staff to his right arm, and they entered the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a woman who beat her breast and cried out:
"Who has committed such an unrighteous and poisonous act as to sever both hands of this bhikṣu?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Sister! My hand was severed by him while I was still a layperson, not after I had gone forth. She replied:
"Who ordained you?
the bhikṣu replied, "My upādhyāya Upānanda."
The upāsikā said, "Aside from those six groups of shameless practitioners of evil conduct, who else could have converted such people?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"O Bhikṣus! All such transgressions arise from ordaining those who are incomplete."
Who are those called "incomplete"?
They are those who are handless, fingerless, footless, cleft-lipped, or lipless, as well as those with impaired faculties; none of these are suitable.
"If one ordains such a person, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
As for those who have been flogged, or whose bodies are mottled with white, or who are too old or too young," the Buddha said:
"One should not ordain them; one must not grant the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha to anyone who is defiled.

Furthermore, those with clubfeet, green eyes, those who are blind, those with hunchbacks, dwarfs, those with goiters on their necks, the mute, the deaf, and those afflicted by dropsy—such as these should all not be ordained."
If one were to ordain such a person, they would incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Furthermore, those who have excessively indulged in sexual desire and been wounded by women;

those who, due to such severe injuries, suffer physical impairment while traveling on the road; and those who cannot control their bowel and bladder movements—such individuals as these should likewise not be ordained.
"If one ordains such a person, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"There are those afflicted with ringworm, scabies, sores, leprosy, fistulas, dry eczema, moist eczema, emaciation, coughing, asthma, parching thirst, malaria, insanity, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids."
The Buddha said:
